t: Jimothy's D10 Isekai JRPG is a tabletop roleplaying game played with ten-sided dice. One player is the Storyteller, who describes the world, plays everyone the characters meet, and keeps the story moving. Everyone else plays a character of their own making. Together you decide what your characters attempt, and the dice decide how well it goes.

The Slime King arrived in Terrana about 150 years ago. In that time the world has advanced in technology, science, and magic until it holds many of the comforts of the 20th and 21st centuries of our own world. It is a mismatch of all kinds, adapted around one key difference: where our world struggles with fuel and power, Terrana uses magic in their place. Terrana has come a long way from the world it once was.
The book is organized so you can read what you need, when you need it.

Chapters 1 through 5 cover Terrana itself: where it came from ( Chapter 1 ), its lands and the settings you can play in ( Chapter 2 ), the island nation of Monsera ( Chapter 3 ), the Grand Dungeon ( Chapter 4 ), and the Legends of Terrana, the names at the top of the world's rankings ( Chapter 5 ). Many lore sections are written by Liris Kant of Monsera University, a scholar who has spent a career studying the peoples and places of Terrana. Read them for flavor and for the things your character would already know. Rules sections are written plainly and are marked by their headings.

Chapter 6 walks through character creation one step at a time, in order. Chapters 7 through 11 hold the options for each step: Chapter 7 : Tropes, Virtues, and Vices Chapter 8 : Heritages Chapter 9 : Merits and Flaws Chapter 10 : Backgrounds Chapter 11 : Willpower, Fate, Sanity, and Mana Keep a character sheet beside you and fill it in as you go. For a first session, a player only needs Chapter 6 and the chapters it points to. Everything else can be read as it comes up at the table.

Chapters 12 and 13 cover the rules used during play: Martial Combat Styles ( Chapter 12 ) and Magic ( Chapter 13 ), including the seven casting schools, Battle Aura, and resurrection. They are written for quick lookup in the middle of a session. Chapter 14 covers Equipment and Items, with loot tables, Chapter 15 is a Bestiary of creatures, monster peoples, and bosses with stat blocks, and Chapter 16 covers Alternate Eras for games set in Terrana's past or future. Key terms and conditions are gathered in the index at the end of the book, followed by the battle maps and the combat playmat (each in a light and a dark version), the Summoner's Sheet, and the character sheet.

This system is still growing, and play is how it improves. When a rule is unclear, feels off, or does not cover something that happened at your table, flag it. Note the chapter and section, what came up, and how your table handled it in the moment, then pass it along to Jimothy. Specific notes like these shape the next version of the book.

Terrana was not born as one world. It was forged from the ruins of six. From “On the Nature of Worlds” by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University People often ask me what the world is. The short answer is that ours is not the only world that ever existed. It is the only one left. There were six, once, joined around a seventh place at their center. Five were destroyed in the God Wars. Their survivors came here, to the Hyuman World, and brought their peoples, their magic, and their grudges with them. Terrana is what grew from that. Some of what follows is recorded history. Some is theory from my colleagues at the university. Some is faith. I have tried to mark which is which, and where the record runs out, I say so.

Before recorded history, six worlds existed together. Each was its own complete reality with its own peoples, cultures, and magic: the Hyuman World, the Beast World, the Demon World, the Dragon World, the Sky World, and the Sea World. The six were joined like bubbles pressed around a smaller seventh at their center. That center was the Void. Potent magic held the structure together. The walls where the worlds met were flat, while every outer surface stayed round. Scholars call the whole structure the Six-Faced World.

The Hyuman God went missing. Something took his place: an impostor now called the Man God, who claimed his title and his authority. The Man God murdered Lunaria, wife of the Dragon God and sister of the Hyuman God, and arranged for the gods of the other worlds to take the blame. In his grief, the Dragon God went to war. One by one, the Dragon World, the Demon World, the Beast World, the Sea World, and the Sky World were destroyed. The Hyuman World survived because it sat on the far side of the structure, the hardest of the six to reach. When the fighting ended, the survivors of the five fallen worlds fled there. They brought their heritages, their traditions, their magic, and their grief. The Hyuman World took them all in, and it became Terrana. The impostor did not escape what he started. The Man God, known by the name Hitogami, is bound in the Void, and he remains there today. Some of this history is left uncertain on purpose. The Followers of Milis worship the Hyuman God as though he were the God of Creation, and the faithful and the scholars of Terrana do not always agree on what happened or why. Mysticism and faith have as much room in Terrana as the university's records do.

Five of the six outer worlds are gone. What remains are two bubbles pressed flat against each other: Terrana on top and the Void World beneath it. The land of Terrana sits on the shared wall between them. Mana passes freely back and forth through that wall. Most of the Void is formless creation energy, the source of all mana. It takes no shape until someone gives it one, which is what a mage does when casting a spell. Monsera University's current theory holds that the Void contains two kinds of mana, and that magic is what happens when the two fuse. It is the best explanation anyone has offered so far, but it remains a theory.

When Hitogami lost his hold on the Void, it split into regions. In two of them, belief takes shape. Stories, dreams, and fears that enough people believe strongly enough take form there, and a character believed in hard enough can appear as a living being. The Dreeming: Where Terrana itself looks like a grounded anime world, the Dreeming is wonky and cartoonish, a place of crooked towers, oversized mushrooms, and landscapes that bend like the pages of an old children's comic. Kind and wondrous beliefs come to life here, and the fey who thrive in it are generally good-natured. The Seeming: The Seeming is a nightmarish hellscape where fears and dark tales are made real. Its landscape is grotesque, and the things that thrive there are the self-serving ones. The two must stay in balance, but the Seeming does not rest. Its corruption almost always works toward ways of taking over the Dreeming, and the border between them is under constant pressure. Beyond them lies the rest of the Void, raw and formless. Somewhere within it, Hitogami remains bound.

Above Terrana's surface is a vast sky, and above the sky is space. Space holds other worlds, other peoples, and monarchies that rule whole regions of it. In the present day, the people of Terrana know none of this.

This book's default setting is Terrana as it is today, but the system is built to carry a game into any era of the world's history. The Distant Past: A game set long ago, during or just after the Great Hyuman-Demon War: a dark age of war, kingdoms, and swords. A Fallen Future: A post-apocalyptic Terrana where today's modern technology has become a collection of ancient relics. The Space Era: A researcher at Monsera discovers that the energy signal of the Rift matches energy coming from far out in the sky. The Hero Rangers Corps forms a sky division to travel to other planets and connect their peoples. Games in this era take place hundreds to a thousand years after that discovery. In the Space Era, ships are common, though never cheap. Many planets and species are friendly to the Hero Rangers Corps, and some are not. Mercenary crews fly for hire under the Mercenaries Guild, much as adventurers work under the Adventurers Guild today, while space monarchies rule their own corners of the sky. Terrana itself remains playable throughout. The closest anyone has come to the source of the Rift's signal is Nyxhollow, a planet full of the voidlings that sometimes break into Terrana. Its energy resembles the Rift's, but the signal leads much further, into the deepest reaches of space. The full details of the Space Era and the other alternate eras are in Chapter 16 .

From “On Arriving” by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University Souls from other worlds sometimes arrive in Terrana. The scholarly term is displacement reincarnation. Nearly everyone else says isekai. It has happened for as long as there are records. Most arrive as infants. Some arrive as children. A few arrive as adults and wake somewhere unfamiliar with no idea how they got there. What they bring varies. Some bring memories of their old lives. Some bring knowledge of things this world had never seen. Some bring nothing but themselves. The Slime King is the best-known case and, by general agreement, the most extreme. Monsera University's Special Students program exists to find and support others like him. In my experience, most of them settle in well.

Five continents, two island realms, and one sea that ties them together. From “A Survey of the Known World” by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University Most people in Terrana never travel far from where they were born, and many hold firm opinions about places they have never seen. This survey describes the lands as my colleagues and I have found them, from the frozen north of the Central Continent to the bogs of the Demon Continent. Borders move and rulers change. Where something here is out of date by the time you read it, I ask for the reader's patience. The coastlines, at least, have held still for a long time. Terrana is made up of seven major landmasses around the Ringus Sea: the Central, Demon, Milis, Begaritt, and Heaven Continents, the island nation of Monsera, and the Shaded Isles. The Merfolk and Fishfolk hold the waters between them.

The largest landmass in Terrana and home to the greatest share of its Hyuman population. The Red Dragon Mountain Range splits the continent into three regions: the North, the West, and the South. The Dragon King Mountain Range runs down its southeastern side, with dense forest along its slopes.

A frozen, unforgiving expanse where survival depends on willpower and magical innovation. The Three Magic Kingdoms: Ranoa, Neris, and Basherant were historically centers of traditional magical learning in a cold and difficult region. Today they are modernizing quickly, using mana-powered heating networks and agricultural magic imported from Monsera to tame their climate. Their partnership with Monsera University is one of the most productive academic relationships in the world. The Kingdom of Biheiril: Set among the northeastern forests and mountains, this Hyuman kingdom keeps long-standing ties with the Ogres of the nearby islands. Its deepest woods shelter the continent's only Superd settlement, a fierce and insular people who protect the realm from threats beyond Hyuman capability while the kingdom leaves them to live as they choose. The Holy Land of the Sword: A land of permanent winter in the far northwest, devoted entirely to mastering the Silver Arc Style of long blades. Many who hope to win the title of Sword God come here to train. It remains stubborn, deeply traditional, and largely unchanged by time. The Ogre Islands: A chain of islands off the northeastern coast and the ancestral home of the island Ogres. Most of its people train to master the Ten Count Style of boxing or the Drifting Leaf Style of kung fu.

The most fertile and prosperous region on the continent, dominated by the Asura Kingdom, the most powerful Hyuman nation in the world. A Modern Kingdom: Once an absolute monarchy, Asura is now a constitutional monarchy governed by a parliament. The royal family functions mainly as high-society celebrities and ceremonial figureheads. Merit-based inheritance rules mean titles do not automatically pass to the eldest child. The Capital City of Ars: The political and economic heart of the nation, governed as its own district apart from the four regions. Ars is the largest and most populous city in the Hyuman world and the seat of both the royal family and parliament. Outside the capital, the kingdom is divided into four regions, each traditionally overseen by a branch of the Greyrat noble line: The Fittoa Region (Northeast): Ruled by the Boreas Greyrat family. An agricultural and pastoral frontier anchored by its administrative hub and fortress city, Roa. The Milbots Region (East): Governed by the Notos Greyrat family. It sits along key routes and serves as the kingdom's main gateway for continental trade. The Donati Region (Northwest): Overseen by the Zephyrus Greyrat family. A strategic and agricultural anchor for the northern borders. The Wisiru Region (South): Governed by the Euros Greyrat family. The southern territory is known for its distinct climate, geography, and natural resources.

A fractured territory defined by a stark divide between lawless chaos and corporate rule. The Strife Zone: The northern half of the region is an ungoverned wilderness of tribal towns caught in permanent, low-level warfare. Void Openings breach here more often than anywhere else on the continent. It has become a haven for insular, low-tech refugee villages escaping the corporate regimes to the south. Monsera has recently made strides in outreach by opening small schools for any child born in the zone. Breakwater: On the coast just east of the Strife Zone sits Breakwater, Monsera's military port and trade gateway on the continent. It is described in full in Chapter 3 . The Corporate Kingdoms: Shirone (Rone Co.), Kikka (Kik Co.), and Sanika (Ani Co.) keep the appearance of crowns and noble titles, but real legislative power belongs to corporate CEOs and boards of directors. Society is divided by literal walls into three tiers: Shareholders, Managers, and Laborers, with perimeter walls built to keep workers from escaping. Decades of suppressed revolutions have left their working districts in ruins. The Dragon King Kingdom: At the southern tip of the continent, this proud monarchy is the trade bridge between Monsera's southern operations and the Begaritt Continent, with East Port and West Port handling most of that traffic. It is the third most powerful nation in the world and has modernized modestly while keeping its cultural identity.

A harsh land east of the Ringus Sea. Its ambient mana density is higher than anywhere else in Terrana, which makes for deadly terrain and some of the most dangerous monsters in the world. The continent is divided into ten domains, each ruled by an Immortal Demon King, and all of them honor the title of the Empress. Most trade with the rest of the world passes through Kurasuma in the northwest and through Wind Port and Zanto Port in the south. Migurd Village, home of the Migurd, and the city of Rikarisu both sit in the northeast.

The chaotic, current Empress of the Demon World, brought to this realm by Necross Lacross during the God Wars. She is volatile, but legendary for her generosity, and has been known to gift one of her coveted Magic Eyes to those who help her. The Magic Eyes and how a character can earn one appear in Chapter 9 .

Badigadi, Biegoya: The husband of Kishirika Kishirisu, known across realms as the Fighting God and the Wise Demon King. His domain of Biegoya lies in the far northeast. Badigadi is one of the few beings the Slime King treats as a peer. Beethove Tovetha, the Library Labyrinth: A monstrous black slime-octopus that rules the Library Labyrinth in the north, using its own ink and tentacles to record every piece of written lore in the world. Raja Iblis Baglahagla: The pig-like King of the Orcs, whose domain covers the northwest of the continent. Vita, the Abyssal King: A parasitic blue slime-demon ruling a domain in the west. Anyone who ingests Vita suffers blinding illusions and visions while Vita takes complete control of their mind and body. Necross Lacross: A renowned tactician of several ancient conflicts who fought in the God Wars, and father to Atoferatofe and Badigadi. His domain lies at the heart of the continent. Atoferatofe Ryback, Gaslow: A terrifying combatant and sister to Badigadi. She is infamous for kidnapping foreign royalty and challenging powerful warriors; those she defeats are conscripted as her “disciples.” Her domain, Gaslow, is a dark bog in the east, and a dark dragon is often seen flying over it. Lynebyne, the Stone King: Ruler of a domain in the southwest of the continent. Samedynomedy, Demon King of Light: Ruler of a domain in the south. Patorsetor, the Enchantress Demon King: Ruler of a domain on the southeastern coast. Qeblaqabla, the Evil Demon King: A floating orb leaking black liquid, ruling a domain at the continent's southern end.

The First Demon God: The multi-armed, six-horned progenitor of many immortal demons, slain during the God Wars. Kirisis Calisis: The First Empress. Malta: The Ogre God. Laplace: The Demon God, born of demon and dragon blood.

Southeast of Monsera, the Milis Continent is split in two by the jagged Blue Dragon Mountain Range. The Great Forest: The northern expanse and the ancestral home of the Beastfolk, whose territory covers most of the forest. The Holy Sword Highway runs through it, connecting the north of the continent to the south. Elf Territory: In the forest's eastern reaches, the reclusive Elves live in balance between nature and some of the most advanced technology Monsera has produced. Halfling Territory: On the hilly western coast, the Halflings have adopted small amounts of technology while staying close to their traditional roots. Dwarf Territory: Along the northern side of the Blue Dragon Mountains, the Dwarves have taken a great interest in steam power. The technology started in Monsera, but the Dwarves have embraced it more than any other recent advancement. The Holy Milis Kingdom: The southern expanse, with its capital at Milishion, and the seat of the Church of Milis. It is the second most powerful nation in Terrana and a genuinely integrated society, with Hyumans and Beastfolk each making up roughly half the population. The Holy Church of Milis, the royal families, and parliament form three co-equal branches of government, though historically the Church has had the greatest say.

A lawless, treacherous landmass in the southwest with no unified government. It is populated almost entirely by adventurers, outlaws, and those who wish to live outside the reach of any state. The continent is defined by its dangerous concentration of shifting Labyrinths and volatile magical anomalies. Labyrinth Town Rapan: On the southern coast, the town of Rapan is built within the ribs of an enormous Behemoth skeleton and serves as the main base for those who delve the continent's Labyrinths.

A sheer plateau resting three thousand meters above sea level in the north. It is home to the Skyfolk, winged, elf-like people whose aloof and detached outlook often makes them seem alien to outsiders. The Hell Dungeon: Beneath the plateau lies the Hell Dungeon, a rift descending through nine layers. It is described in full in the section that follows.

The Hell Dungeon is a nine-layered rift beneath the Heaven Continent. Each layer is its own kingdom, ruled by a devil prince or queen, and together they make up what most of Terrana simply calls Hell. It is not to be confused with the Grand Dungeon of Monsera, though the naming has caused confusion before.

For as long as anyone can remember, Hell has run on suffering. Devils harvest mana from pain, fear, and despair, and the old powers of Hell built their kingdoms on that harvest. About sixty years ago, Sciel, Queen of the third layer, proved that devils can harvest and regenerate mana just as well from happiness and other positive emotions. She left Hell before the fighting truly began and, with the Slime King's help, founded Nite City in the Grand Dungeon, which has been a refuge for fleeing devils ever since. Mahk, whose true name is Belethore, once ruled the second layer. He left as well, and today he runs the CCN's studios hidden in the Grand Dungeon. Their departures shook Hell to its foundations.

s: The War for the Old Ways
t: Zagan, Prince of the fourth layer, saw the new way of living as a threat to everything Hell was built on. He launched a war of conquest to unite Hell under his rule and preserve the old ways of suffering. His forces took the fifth layer and captured its queen, Gremory, and the sixth layer's ruler, Marchosias, now serves under him. The second and third layers, left without their rulers, are now governed by Mahk's cousin, also named Belethore. He rules as Zagan's puppet, and with both layers under Zagan's control in all but name, the fighting has come to a standstill. Total chaos has been avoided in recent times through the diplomatic efforts of Monsera's Slime King. Not every layer has fallen in line. Phenex of the seventh layer, Eligor of the eighth, and Astaroth of the ninth rule independently, and the three work together to keep Zagan's forces from conquering any further up into Hell. The seventh layer, bordering Marchosias's domain, is almost always in a constant state of battle. Lucifer of the first layer also remains independent. The calm is not peace. Zagan has turned his attention to the world outside Hell, and his agents work to cause mayhem across Terrana. Layer Ruler Status 1 Lucifer Independent 2 Belethore (Mahk's cousin) Zagan's puppet. Formerly ruled by Mahk (Belethore), who left for the Grand Dungeon 3 Belethore (Mahk's cousin) Zagan's puppet. Formerly ruled by Sciel, who founded Nite City 4 Zagan Seat of the would-be conqueror of Hell 5 Held by Zagan Conquered; its queen, Gremory, is his captive 6 Marchosias Serves under Zagan 7 Phenex Independent. Allied with layers 8 and 9 against Zagan; almost always at war 8 Eligor Independent. Allied with layers 7 and 9 against Zagan 9 Astaroth Independent. Allied with layers 7 and 8 against Zagan

The island nation of Monsera sits in the southern Ringus Sea, between the Central Continent and the Milis Continent. It is the technological and magical center of modern Terrana. Its history and institutions are covered in full in Chapter 3 . The Capital: A sprawling metropolis governed by a guild-based parliamentary democracy and home to the world-renowned Monsera University. The Grand Dungeon and Arena: Just east of the capital. The grand colosseum above is owned by the citizens of Monsera, while the 100-floor Dungeon below is co-owned by the Slime King and the Earth God. No adventuring party has ever cleared the final ten floors. The Dungeon is covered in Chapter 4 . Hero Rangers HQ: On the island's north shore stands the headquarters of the Hero Rangers Corps, who guard the world against the Rift.

A mist-shrouded archipelago east of Monsera. The isles are part of the Monsera nation, much as an outlying island belongs to its mainland, but they are home to three ancient, sovereign noble houses of the Undead. The Vampiric Kingdom: The largest of the isles, ruled by an ancient house of Vampires. The Dullahan Kingdom: Southeast of the Vampiric Kingdom, ruled by a noble house of Dullahans. The Liches' Domain: Just south of the Vampiric Kingdom, ruled by a noble house of Liches.

s: The Ringus Sea and Surrounding Waters
t: The stormy central ocean that connects every land in Terrana, and the open waters beyond its coasts. The Rift: A permanent, catastrophic tear into the Void at the center of the sea. About once a year it ruptures and releases a Kaiju-class threat. These disasters are held back by the Hero Rangers Corps alone, operating from their stronghold on Monsera's north shore.

The waters of Terrana belong to the Merfolk and the Fishfolk. Merfolk prefer the central waters of the Ringus Sea, while Fishfolk prefer the northern and southern waters. The two peoples intermingle and intermarry freely, but each tribe answers to its own sovereign Chieftain.

An island of monsters that became the most advanced nation in the world. From “A Survey of the Known World” by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University I have lived and taught in Monsera for most of my career, which makes it the hardest place in this survey to describe fairly. Visitors notice the lights, the trains, and the screens. Residents notice that a goblin, a harpy, and a Hyuman can sit at the same lunch counter and nobody looks twice. Both observations are true. Monsera is the most technologically advanced civilization in Terrana. The island sits in the southern Ringus Sea and was once home to a fractured, tribal collection of monster peoples. Today it is a city-nation that does not fit any older category. Its look sits somewhere between a modern New York, a neon Tokyo, and a late-1990s vision of the future. The public transit network is efficient and covers the whole island. The Crystalz Communication Network (CCN) puts a personal communication and data device in the hands of nearly every citizen. Because of the particular interests of its ruler, video game technology has reached a level that mirrors the PlayStation 1 and Nintendo 64 era of another world. Education is treated as a basic right: Monsera University charges no tuition and pays its students a stipend.

About 150 years ago, the being now known as the Slime King arrived in Terrana as a blind, senseless slime. He spent his first decade in total sensory deprivation, holding on to his sanity through a single desire to play video games again and the help of his Great Sage ability. His real work began only once his Awareness grew strong enough to perceive his surroundings. The twenty years that followed were defined by diplomacy rather than conquest. The Slime King moved among the island's warring monster factions, learned their fears, desires, and cultures, and bargained with them until the tribes agreed to unite. Over the next two decades, the foundations of modern Monsera were laid. Foreign empires watched from a distance and dismissed the island as “Monster Island.” Earlier colonial attempts by Hyuman kingdoms had failed badly against its territorial and diverse monster populations. They did not expect a leader who rejected colonialism entirely and chose integration instead. About a hundred years ago, Monsera opened its first global trade routes and diplomatic ties, and the outside world was forced to recognize it as a sovereign power. Everything that defines the modern setting was built during the century that followed: the university, the CCN, the Grand Dungeon, the Guild Cabinet, and the Hero Rangers Corps.

s: The Slime King: Julius Geoffrey Golbjorn
t: Before his reincarnation, Geoffrey was a computer science student in Stockholm, Sweden. On November 1st, 1997, the Swedish release date of Final Fantasy VII, he was struck and killed by a moving van while crossing the street, reading the game manual he had waited in line to buy. He died holding the game without ever having played a second of it. Monsera is the direct result of that loss. To play video games, Geoffrey needed screens. To make screens, he needed an industrial supply chain. To support manufacturing, he needed global infrastructure, an advanced civilization, and a highly educated population. Today he sits on a beanbag chair in the royal suite of Monsera Palace, playing video games. His current grand project is an exact reconstruction of Final Fantasy VII, the game that got away, carried out through the university's Special Students program and its research into memory extraction.

s: Storyteller Note: How Powerful Is the Slime King?
t: This is not a stat block for play. It tells the Storyteller how far beyond any player character the Slime King stands, in case a group ever decides to fight him. Concept: Singular Minded. Motivation: Gaming. Power: Treat every one of his traits as if it were at 10, beyond the normal maximum. He has every Merit in existence and, for all practical purposes, unlimited mana. Standing: Legendary Immortals such as Badigadi treat him as a peer. He is officially ranked the second most powerful being in the world, just behind the Dragon God, a ranking he completely ignores.

An elite academy open to every heritage in Terrana, with free tuition and a baseline stipend for every student. Its curriculum pairs traditional fields with leading magical research, including combat training, magical theory, time manipulation, and dreamwalking. The Special Students Homeroom: A class for misfits, political outliers, and uniquely gifted students, overseen by Professor Malakai Nocturne. Combat and Ethics: Led by Professor Aldric Thorne, an esteemed master who holds the title of Water God.

The backbone of communication in Terrana. Handheld Personal Crystalz work much like smartphones, while large stationary Crystalz serve as flat-screen televisions. The network runs on a combination of crafted Magical Implements and self-recharging Magical Artifacts. It covers all of Monsera and reaches foreign population centers through major trade relays.

A multinational military corps backed jointly by the leaders of the seven most powerful kingdoms in the world. The HRC works with every nation in Terrana and keeps outposts in all of them. It is run with the discipline of an army and the organization of a large institution, and in the public eye it holds a place much like a space agency in our world: its top operatives are celebrities and its equipment is the most advanced in existence. The HRC accepts anyone. Its core belief is that there is no such thing as one true hero, and that true strength comes in numbers. Many recruits are people who felt lost, or who always wanted to be a hero, and the Corps gives them focus, purpose, and a place to call home.

s: The Rift and the Seafolk Barrier
t: The Rift at the center of the Ringus Sea is a permanent opening into the Void. Seafolk mages maintain a barrier over it that holds back most of what tries to come through. Energy from the Void still builds up beneath the barrier, and from time to time it gathers into monsters strong enough to break through. Left unchecked, swarms of these smaller monsters can overwhelm Seafolk cities and drive their people from the water, and from there the monsters become a problem for the land. Roughly once a year, something far larger forms: a Kaiju-class threat rising from the floor of the Ringus Sea. Stopping both is the HRC's primary mission.

The HRC is divided into five branches, each identified by a color and a specialty. Branches train separately and focus on their own fields, but they always work together. Platoons are usually made up of equal numbers from all five branches, and aboard a ship each branch runs its own section. Red Branch (Army): Leadership, command, and front-line coordination. Yellow Branch (Navy): Science, research, analysis, and technology. Green Branch (Marines): Nature, survival, field medicine, and work in the wild. Blue Branch (Air Force): Physics, engineering, flight, and heavy machinery. Violet Branch (Coast Guard): Law, order, protection of civilians, and defensive operations.

HRC ranks run from 1 to 7, matching the F to S letter ranks used across Terrana. Each rank up is far smaller than the one below it. Rank Who Holds It How Many Rank 1 (F) Trainees still in basic training. Varies with each recruiting season Rank 2 (E) The official starting rank for every full member of the Corps. Many thousands Rank 3 (D) The backbone of the Corps and the most common rank. The largest group Rank 4 (C) Experienced operatives, specialists, and squad leaders. A few thousand Rank 5 (B) Senior officers and elite specialists. A few hundred Rank 6 (A) Ship captains, generals, and high command. Most are either a new generation striving to reach Rank 7, or former Rank 7s who stepped down after aging out of piloting and whose expertise is still invaluable. A few dozen Rank 7 (S) The only rank eligible to try out to pilot a Titan. Usually 10: five main pilots and five understudies, ready if a main pilot is hurt

Hero Team 6 is stationed permanently on Monsera. Its mission is to deal with the huge and gargantuan Kaiju that rise from the Ringus Sea before they can reach any shore. For years the team fought in enhanced combat suits. Now, after decades of research, the HRC has unveiled the Titans.

Red Ranger, Captain Ralden Veyr: A veteran knight-commander and inspiring battlefield leader. Confident and charismatic, the poster face of the Corps. Yellow Ranger, Dr. Selene Quen: A scholar-mage and technologist. Pragmatic and sharp-witted, and openly nerdy when something excites her. Green Ranger, Lyra Fernbrook: A druidic envoy from the Deepwild. Grounded, spiritual, and protective of balance. Blue Ranger, Professor Dorrim Korr: A Dwarven physicist and engineer. Gruff and blunt, and explains everything in simple, physical terms. Violet Ranger, Magistrate Althis Kael: A judge and legislator of the High Courts. Formal and righteous, and speaks in measured tones.

The Titans are giant combat units built to fight Kaiju at sea and keep them from reaching the coast. This is the first generation, and each unit is fitted with programs for its pilot's specialty so the team fights best together. Unit 01, Crimson Dragon (Red): An eastern-style sea dragon built for command. Command Roar: a concussive roar that staggers Kaiju and rallies allies. Firestorm Breath: a sweeping arc of fire that drives Kaiju away from the coast. Battlefield Coordination: its glowing horns project tactical sigils into the sky that link the other Titans. Unit 02, Golden Chimera (Yellow): A lion with hawk wings and a serpent tail, built for experimentation. Analyzing Eye: scans Kaiju for weak points, toxins, and mutations. Adaptive Arsenal: shifts its elemental attacks to match the weaknesses it finds. Winged Maneuverability: aerial scouting and precise strikes. Unit 03, Emerald Treant-Beast (Green): A colossal stag fused with a living tree. Root Snare: roots and vines rise from the ground or sea floor to bind Kaiju. Healing Sap: restorative pollen clouds that repair allies. Antler Charge: glowing antlers that ram or impale with brutal force. Unit 04, Azure Leviathan (Blue): A giant armored sea serpent and whale hybrid that fights with raw physics. Gravity Crash: crushing gravitational pulses that pin Kaiju or add weight to its blows. Wave Manipulation: tail strikes that raise waves or redirect currents to keep Kaiju offshore. Sonic Resonance: a deep bellow that throws Kaiju off balance. Unit 05, Amethyst Knight (Violet): A towering, rune-carved armored knight. Binding Edict: glowing chains of runes that immobilize Kaiju. Judgment Blade: a massive crystal sword that cuts through Kaiju armor and burns brighter the more chaotic its target. Barrier of Order: magical shields that protect civilians and allies.

When all five units unite, they form a single colossal warrior that embodies leadership, science, nature, physics, and law. Its ultimate attack, the Edict of Balance, is a reality-rending strike that both destroys a Kaiju and restores balance to the battlefield. Because the Titans are newly unveiled, the Edict has not yet been used in battle.

Monsera is a guild-based parliamentary democracy in which the King serves as a ceremonial figurehead. Every citizen aged 18 or older has the right to join a guild, and guild membership is how a citizen gains a political voice. Seats in the parliamentary cabinet are divided among ten core guilds. The Ten Cabinet Guilds: Adventurers, Arts, Makers, Merchants, Mages, Farmers, Healers, Scholars, Laborers, and Navigators. The Thieves Guild: Extralegal and unrepresented on paper. This shadow faction holds no parliamentary seat and operates through its own secure dialect, Thieves' Cant.

The headquarters of the Hero Rangers Corps stands on Monsera's north shore, facing the Rift. Hero Team 6 and the Titans are based here, and it hosts the annual summit of the United Domains of Terrana.

Founded on the east coast of the Central Continent, beside the Strife Zone, Breakwater is Monsera's main military port. It was built first to cut response times to Void Breaches in the Strife Zone and second to serve as a major trade gateway. The city has a high-energy New Orleans feel and a majority monster population, with every heritage in the world represented. All ten cabinet guilds keep a strong presence here alongside a permanent detachment of the Hero Rangers Corps. Breakwater is the cornerstone of Monsera's long-term plan to expand its presence onto the Central Continent peacefully. A Refugee Haven: Escapees from the Corporate Kingdoms arrive constantly and are granted automatic asylum. Anyone can claim their freedom here, though the paranoia drilled into refugees by corporate conditioning means it often takes years before they truly believe they are safe.

The misty archipelago east of the main island is part of the Monsera nation, though its three undead noble houses govern themselves. See Chapter 2 for the Vampiric Kingdom, the Dullahan Kingdom, and the Liches' Domain.

An annual summit held at Hero Rangers HQ. It is not a world government but a high-stakes diplomatic council. Any recognized sovereign nation may send a voting member to debate cross-continental magical incidents, trade blockades, Void Openings, and coming Kaiju threats. Its rulings are not binding, but they carry great diplomatic weight.

Monsera's economic influence has standardized currency across the major trade routes. This table converts standard coins into Mana Crystals, the lifeblood of magical craft and commerce. The values in our world's dollars are for the table's reference only. Coin Value (USD Equivalent) Mana Crystal Equivalent Scale of Use Small Copper $0.10 Mana Crystal Dust Minor daily items Large Copper $1.00 Mana Crystal Shards Standard daily goods Small Silver $10.00 Small Mana Crystals Modest gear and services Large Silver $100.00 Mana Crystals High-end equipment and weapons Small Gold $1,000.00 Large Mana Crystals Rare artifacts and property Large Gold $10,000.00 Huge Mana Crystals Major investments King's Gold $100,000.00 Sovereign-Reserve Crystals State-level transfers only

One hundred floors down, and every one of them is open for business. From “A Survey of the Known World” by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University Most dungeons in Terrana are dangerous accidents of mana and time. The Grand Dungeon is dangerous on purpose. It sits just east of Monsera's capital beneath the great colosseum, and it is the only dungeon I know of with a staff roster, a payroll, and a complaints department. I have been as far as the seventy-fifth floor. I went no further, and I do not regret it. The Grand Dungeon spans exactly one hundred floors. It is co-owned by the Slime King and the Earth God, a fairy-type Immortal Demon King who serves as its creative director. She redesigns floor layouts regularly so that veteran delvers never grow too comfortable. Because she has no interest in day-to-day logistics, a large company runs the dungeon's daily operations under her supervision. No adventuring party has ever cleared the final ten floors.

Access to the dungeon is strictly regulated. The entry turnstiles will not turn for anyone without a dungeon bracelet. The bracelets do not belong to any guild. They are issued and regulated by the Arena above the dungeon, which is owned by the Kingdom of Monsera, so no single guild is responsible for keeping the dungeon's rules.

Every ten floors form one stretch with two biomes. The first biome runs from the first floor of the stretch to the fourth, and its last floor ends at a mini-boss who must be defeated before delvers can enter the safe zone on the fifth floor. The second biome runs from the sixth floor to the tenth, where a boss guards the way down. The floors grow smaller the deeper you go, but they never become small. The upper floors hold open fields and whole cities, and even the deepest floors are wide enough to hold landscapes of their own. The hundredth floor is a single massive arena. The one exception is the final stretch. Floors 91 through 100 form a single biome with no safe zone on the ninety-fifth floor.

Every floor ending in five is a safe zone and a permanent community. Reaching a safe zone for the first time unlocks its teleporter for you. Teleporters connect only safe zones, so fast travel is possible only between them. Every safe zone enforces the same three laws, kept by Golem Guards: 1. No bloodshed. 2. No theft. 3. No harmful spells. Breaking any of these laws results in immediate punishment. Nite City, on the fifteenth floor, is the one place where the laws bend; see its entry.

Every delver is assigned a respawn locker on the surface, and their bracelet holds a mana crystal linked to that locker. The bracelet works only in the Grand Dungeon. It does nothing anywhere else in Terrana, and no other dungeon has anything like it. As long as they wear a bracelet, no one can die in the Grand Dungeon. When a character is Incapacitated and no one heals them back up on the very next turn, their body vanishes. The bracelet consumes its mana crystal and teleports them to their locker on the surface. Because of this, no one in the dungeon can ever choose Blaze of Glory or Risk It. Respawning does not fully heal a character. Remove all of their Lethal and Aggravated damage, so they never have to worry about a missing limb or a huge scar, then mark every Bashing box, even if their Bashing track was not full when they fell. A character who cannot heal will be in pain for a while, but a night of rest usually sets them right. Their personal teleport destination also resets to the nearest safe zone above the floor where they fell.

The Inhabitants: The monsters roaming the floors are paid employees of the dungeon company. When defeated, they respawn and return to their living quarters on the nearest safe zone. The Loot: The company buys the treasures placed throughout the floors. Over time, the high ambient mana inside the dungeon gives these well-made items unpredictable, random magical properties.

Wide stone corridors lit by mana lamps, home to slimes, goblins, kobolds, and giant rats. These floors are where every delver learns the basics, and they are always busy with new guild members on their first runs.

A veteran goblin warchief and a dungeon employee of thirty years, Gruk leads a warband that has humbled more fresh parties than any other foe in the dungeon. He fights with a crude cleaver and a lot of shouting, and he respects any party that beats him fairly.

Falsky is the largest floor in the dungeon. A false sky enchantment projects clouds, birds, and warm golden light over rolling fields of grass and wheat, scattered farmsteads, and a market village at its heart. The whole community is built to look the way the world did before the Slime King arrived. Its residents prefer the old ways: shopkeepers, tavern keepers, and farmers dress in the older styles, trade by hand, and keep modern devices out of sight. Some live this way because they love it. Plenty of others work here in costume and go home to the surface at the end of their shift to live ordinary modern lives.
Damp caverns lit by glowing mushrooms the size of houses. Spore clouds, myconid scouts, and cave crawlers make these floors the first real test of a party's endurance.

An open-air stone amphitheater ringed by ironwood trees, its stands packed with off-duty dungeon staff placing bets. The Grand Beastmaster, a high-ranking Orc commander from the Laborers Guild, fights alongside a huge multi-headed chimera. The fight is loud and theatrical, and it tests whether a party can work together before going deeper.

From the moment a party leaves the Colosseum, it enters a single labyrinth that runs all the way to the gates of Nite City. It is difficult to tell which floor you have reached, and entire parties have starved until their bracelets sent them home. Adventurers use a site on the CCN to try to map it, but the Earth God changes the layout so often that a complete map may be impossible.
A minotaur who has walked the Labyrinth longer than any map has existed. Asterion hunts by sound and smell, and he is waiting at the Labyrinth's final gate for anyone who makes it that far.

Hidden in a pocket between Floors 14 and 15, this secret level is the main content production hub for the CCN. It is run by an unusual pair: Mahk the Boiler, whose true name is Belethore and who once ruled the second layer of Hell, and Hea'vee Starve'aey, a Sphinx game show host.

Officially Sciel City, this floor is known to nearly every adventurer as Nite City. It looks like Tokyo, New York, and Las Vegas thrown together, and everything here is cheap and entirely legal. More people live in Nite City than on any other floor, though Falsky covers more ground. Nite City was founded about sixty years ago with the Slime King's help. The Immortal Devil Queen Sciel, once ruler of Hell's third layer, had grown tired of Hell's economy, which runs on mana harvested from suffering. She discovered that devils can harvest and regenerate mana just as well from happy, positive emotions, and she left Hell before its war truly began. Since then the city has been a refuge for devils fleeing the underworld. Every devil living here is under contract to the Slime King and the Earth God. Nite City is the one safe zone where the three laws bend. The devils mostly regulate their own rules here, and the laws are broken more often than anywhere else in the dungeon. It is a wild place, but the locals still frown on anyone fighting openly unless someone is betting on the fight or paying for it. You will hear “gold is king” on every corner, but it is a saying, not a law. The city is governed by a parliament led by an executive Mayor and seven District Heads. Each district is tied to one of the seven scales of virtue and vice. District Scale Current Head Primary Color Secondary Color Obsidian Ring Sloth and Diligence Countess Lazara Black Gray Ruby North Wrath and Patience Prince Phobius Dark Red Bright Red Amber East Gluttony and Temperance Duchess Vainessa Amber Dark Orange Emerald South-East Envy and Kindness Marquess Sinestra Green Teal Sapphire South-West Pride and Humility Duke Carnosus Blue Copper Amethyst West Lust and Chastity Baron Stygian Violet Soft Pink Diamond Central Greed and Charity Mayor Balthazar Gold Alabaster
Below Nite City the stone gives way to brass. Catwalks hang over grinding gears and hissing steam lines, and clockwork guardians patrol on fixed routes. Timing matters more than strength here.

A huge, ancient steam automaton built by the Makers Guild, standing on a brass platform above a sea of gears. It changes the speed of the floor's machinery as it fights, forcing parties to time their movements around shifting platforms and bursting steam pipes while they work to crack its armor.
A rainforest under artificial sunlight, crossed high above the forest floor on branches and vines. Giant insects, gliding predators, and territorial birds make every crossing a risk.
The great thunderbird that rules the canopy. Skyrend dives out of the artificial clouds trailing lightning and knocks careless delvers from the branches.

Hollowed-out redwoods serve as homes and shops, connected by suspension bridges and wooden walkways. A few thousand people live here year-round. It is the main source of fresh alchemy ingredients and monster-taming supplies in the upper dungeon, and the local Adventurers Guild outpost posts monster-tracking bounties for the surrounding floors.

The forest drains into black water. These floors are half-submerged tunnels and drowned halls, where delvers wade, swim, and hold their breath past eels, drowned guardians, and things that wait below the surface.

A deep underwater amphitheater ringed by sharp reefs and sunken galleons, swept by currents strong enough to drag a delver across the floor. The Kraken Vanguard, a huge and intelligent Seafolk champion under contract with the Navigators Guild, fights with sweeping tentacles, ink clouds that blind casters, and whirlpools that split a party apart.
Mine shafts and smelting halls, hot and loud, where ore carts run on their own and golems shamble through the smoke. The heat wears on anyone who lingers.
A walking furnace of riveted plates, built long ago to clear cave-ins and later put to work guarding the way to the Foundry. It is slow, nearly unstoppable, and very hard to hurt from the front.

A retro-industrial dwarven smithy crossed with a modern assembly line, full of automated steam hammers, molten brass channels, and neon schematics projected on soot-stained stone. Its population is mostly smiths and their families, a working town of a couple of thousand. It is the first safe zone with high-grade weapon modification and armor rebuilding, and Makers Guild workshops repair broken gear or melt down scrap loot into raw materials.

s: Floors 36 to 39: The Hall of Illusions
t: Endless galleries and painted halls where doors lead back to where you started, portraits watch you pass, and nothing is quite where it looks to be. Trusting your eyes is the most common mistake on these floors.

An eight-sided ballroom where every wall, floor, and ceiling tile is an unbreakable silver mirror. The Doppler Matriarch, a high-tier devil illusionist from Nite City, creates solid mirror copies of each party member with their exact abilities, and the party must work out which reflection is the real one controlling the rest.
Ruined seaside temples in a vast cavern where an indoor tide rises and falls on a schedule. Delvers have to read the tide tables or be cut off as the water comes in.
The eldest of the ruins' sirens. Her song draws delvers into the rising water, and she is far more dangerous to a party that cannot stop listening.

A seaside pier inside a water-filled cavern, lined with carnival games, neon taverns, and seafood shacks looking out over a glowing indoor ocean with moving tides. About a thousand people live here, many of them Seafolk. The Navigators Guild runs this rest stop, where delvers can hire aquatic guides, buy underwater breathing gear, or gamble their coin at the boardwalk games.
The water ends at fields of cooling lava, ash storms, and steam vents. Fire elementals and salamanders thrive here, and the ground itself is not always safe to stand on.

A circular platform surrounded by pools of magma and roaring smoke extractors, where the heat alone wears delvers down. Cindermaw is a wild fire drake fused with experimental company machinery. It melts parts of the arena as the fight goes on, shrinking the ground a party has left to stand on.
Halls of dark volcanic rock carved with glowing glyphs. Many doors open only for those who can read them, and the wrong answer triggers wards and traps. Scholars do well here.
An ancient guardian covered in shifting runes, posed in front of the Archives' gate. It asks questions before it fights, and parties that answer well find it easier to beat.

A quiet library carved from volcanic rock, where thousands of slate tablets fill towering shelves that slide on brass tracks. Only a few hundred people live here, almost all of them researchers and archivists. The Scholars Guild runs it, and it is a required stop for identifying high-level artifacts or translating coded scripts found below. Delvers can also buy rare spell scrolls or trade historical findings for dungeon credit.
Narrow burial tunnels stacked with crumbling sarcophagi and choked with dust. Undead patrol the dark, and the tight corridors make it hard for ranged fighters to find a clear shot.

A sprawling mausoleum of tight corridors. The Dullahan Overseer, an ancient armored knight representing the noble houses of the Shaded Isles, steps through the shadowed walls to cut off retreat and lets out deadly wails that test a party's mental grit and physical endurance.

s: Floors 61 to 64: The Old Rail Tunnels
t: Abandoned service tunnels from an older version of the dungeon's transit system. Derelict cars, live rails, and scavenging constructs fill the dark, and the occasional train still comes through without warning.
The ghostly conductor of a train that was decommissioned long ago and never stopped running. Kessler fights from his engine and insists that every passenger present a valid ticket.

A crowded Victorian-style subway terminal of black iron and white tile, loud with humming teleporters and commuter trains carrying dungeon staff. Only a couple of hundred people live here; most of the crowd is passing through. It is the main transit station for the dungeon's monster employees. Delvers can visit the Healers Guild clinic for advanced curse removal, use secure bank vaults, or take delivery jobs to the lower floors.
Sealed research wings full of failed experiments, unstable spell circuits, and escaped test subjects. The magic here is volatile, and spells sometimes behave in ways their casters did not intend.

A sealed security hall lined with glowing mana circuits, where the wrong floor tile sets off a burst of lightning. Warden Arcanum, an advanced defense construct built by the Mages Guild, absorbs elemental spells to power its own devastating attacks. Parties must rely on physical strikes and non-magical tricks to shut down its power cores.
Tunnels lined with raw mana crystal that hums and glows. The crystal is valuable and fragile, and so are the creatures made of it.
A great lizard whose hide is a living crystal lattice. Its gaze turns flesh to crystal, and it guards the last approach to the Obsidian Vault.

Sleek corporate minimalism in seamless black obsidian, lit by blue ley-line circuitry. There are no markets here, only a few elite offices run by the Merchants Guild and staffed by a few dozen people. The Vault deals only in gold-tier transactions, rare mana crystal trades, and luxury gear for veteran parties.

No one would be allowed to keep a real Void breach open, so these floors are built to look like one. Gravity shifts, rooms repeat, and constructs modeled after real, carefully studied voidlings stalk the halls. Some of the voidlings here are not constructs at all: the company captures real ones and keeps them contained on these floors.

A narrow, unstable ledge above a convincing replica of a tear in the Void, where howling winds pull at anyone standing too close to the edge. The Rift Stalker is the real thing: a captured multi-dimensional predator, held on this floor by magic barriers that keep it from escaping for everyone's safety. It phases out of reality between its turns and leaves gravity anomalies behind, forcing delvers to balance attacking with keeping their footing.

A mountain temple path of endless stone stairs, shrines, and narrow ledges. Gravity is reversed on these floors, which is how delvers climb the stairs while still traveling downward into the dungeon. The monks who guard it test discipline as much as strength.
A silent Ogre who waits at the top of the final stair. He fights unarmed, never seems to tire, and will not let a party pass until they prove themselves worthy.

The quietest safe zone in the dungeon: a walled garden of white stone on a high mountain floor, holding a single cherry blossom tree whose petals never pile up, raked white gravel, and natural hot springs with healing qualities. Only a handful of keepers live here. There are no shops or bars, only the springs themselves, which heal the body and are dense enough with mana to fully replenish a caster's mana. It is the last place to rest before the final floors, and the last teleporter in the dungeon.
Halls of brimstone and chains, staffed by devils on contract who did not choose Nite City's gentler life. The air is hot and heavy, and the fighting is brutal.

A hanging iron cage in total darkness with nowhere to hide and no room to run. The Devil Prince Defiler, an exile from the Hell Dungeon under personal contract to the Earth God, is a true spellsword. Like most devils he is strongest with magic, hurling hellfire and curses from range, but he is just as dangerous up close with brutal melee combinations. Equally deadly at any distance, he is a pure test of how well a party can take damage and deal it back.

The final stretch is a single descent through the dragon's domain: ancient halls scorched by old fire, piles of bones and treasure, and guardians who have served the same master for centuries. There is no safe zone on the ninety-fifth floor and no teleporter anywhere below Sage's Solitude, so a party must make the whole descent in one push. This is a key reason no party has ever cleared the final floors.

s: Final Boss, Floor 100: The Last Lair
t: The entire hundredth floor is one massive arena of ancient stone, the largest battleground in the dungeon, its edges heaped with glowing mana crystals and historic artifacts. Vaelthrax is an ancient dragon and the Slime King's legendary, undefeated companion. The fight has no gimmicks or environmental tricks: only immense physical strength, near-total immunity to magic, and devastating breath. It is the final exam for anyone who has survived the descent.

Vaelthrax does not spend all his time in his lair. He can take a Hyuman-looking form, and in that form he lives a separate life on the surface under the name Thraxus. He is not a very creative dragon. Very few people know who he really is, and a character could meet him in Monsera without ever realizing it.

Everyone in Terrana knows who is on top. Most of them want to be. From “A Survey of the Known World” by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University Terrana loves a ranking. Taverns argue over them, whole channels on the CCN are devoted to them, and children in Monsera can recite the Seven Strongest before they can recite their letters. I have recorded the three that matter most, with one warning: the bottom of every list changes faster than any book can be printed. Three leaderboards define the peak of power and achievement in Terrana. The Seven Strongest ranks the most powerful beings in the world. The Slime King's Elite Four ranks the strongest warriors of Monsera. The Deep Delver Leaderboard ranks the parties who have gone deepest into the Grand Dungeon. Together they are the goals that drive many ambitious adventurers.

The Seven Strongest is a world-recognized ranking with one strict rule: a God Rank title can only be won by defeating its current holder in combat. The defeated holder drops to Imperial Rank, and the victor takes the title. Because each title carries its rank and passes from holder to holder, the ranking lists titles rather than names. Rank Title Current Holder 1 The Dragon God Known by title alone 2 The Slime King Julius Geoffrey Golbjorn 3 The Fighting God Badigadi 4 The Death God Classified 5 The Sword God Changes often 6 The North God Changes often 7 The Water God Professor Aldric Thorne (currently)
Profile: The son of the first Dragon God, he has walked Terrana since before recorded history. He travels the world alone, keeping an eternal watch against any chance of Hitogami's return.

Holder: Julius Geoffrey Golbjorn, ruler of Monsera. Profile: His power is so far beyond anyone else's that the ranking barely measures it (see the Storyteller Note in Chapter 3 ). He spends most of his time in the royal suite of Monsera Palace playing video games and ignores the ranking completely.

Holder: Badigadi, the Wise Demon King of Biegoya. Profile: An Immortal Demon King with six arms and the devoted husband of Empress Kishirika. He is famous for his love of lively parties and good company.

Holder: Classified. Profile: The Death God's true identity is known only to the king of the Dragon King Kingdom and his highest-ranking generals. The holder is gaunt and wears distinctive, easily recognized armor. Ironically, the Death God hates killing, despite being exceptionally good at it.

Titles: The Sword God, the North God, and the Water God. Profile: Unlike the top four, these titles are always changing hands. They pass back and forth through formal, high-stakes duels and challenge matches across the continents. Monsera University's own Professor Aldric Thorne currently holds the title of Water God.

The Elite Four are the Slime King's personal vanguard. Julius Geoffrey Golbjorn never wanted a personal guard, but during Monsera's early years its monster peoples saw a circle of champion warriors as a great source of pride. Today the Elite Four are the four strongest active citizens of the island nation.

The Festival Tournament: Every year, during the two-week festival celebrating Monsera's founding, the citizens host a huge martial tournament in the Grand Arena. The Gauntlet: The tournament's champion earns the right to challenge the Elite Four. The challenger faces one member at a time over four months, with weeks of rest and training between each duel. Rank Displacement: A challenger who defeats a member of the Elite Four takes that member's rank, and every member below it moves down one place. Anyone pushed out of the Elite Four must win next year's tournament to earn a chance at returning. The Sovereign Right: A challenger who defeats all four members earns the right to challenge the Slime King himself for the throne. The same right goes automatically to anyone who clears all one hundred floors of the Grand Dungeon. Historical Record: Only one challenger has ever defeated the entire Elite Four and faced the King. She lost to the Slime King, but her effort earned her the top place in the Elite Four, which she has held ever since.

Heritage: Devil. Profile: The founder of Sciel City, better known as Nite City, and the only challenger ever to sweep the Elite Four. She earned her place in a legendary fight against the Slime King and has held the top rank ever since.
Heritage: Elder Orc. Profile: A seasoned military veteran and a central pillar of Monsera's internal defense forces.
Heritage: Armored Minotaur. Profile: A powerful warrior who first rose through the ranks of the Laborers Guild.
Heritage: Arachne. Profile: The newest member of the Elite Four, who won her place by taking the most recent annual tournament.

The Deep Delver Leaderboard is a community board on a site on the CCN. It tracks the seven parties who have gone deepest into the Grand Dungeon, and it is updated both by people who work at the Arena and by the wider community. No party has ever cleared the final ten floors, so parties are ranked by the deepest floor they have reached. Only part of the board is verified. A party checks in with the guild each time it reaches a floor ending in five, and those check-ins are the only official record. Anything deeper is known only through the party's own word or the community's. The only reason anyone knows the Ashen Vanguard reached Floor 93 is that they live streamed it. Rank Party Deepest Floor Status 1 The Ashen Vanguard 93 (live streamed) Active 2 The Void Walkers 90 Retired 3 The Copper Coin Syndicate 87 Active 4 The Silver Horizon 85 or deeper Unknown 5 Nebula's Edge 85 Active 6 The Ironwood Cartel 82 Disbanded 7 The Chimera Pack 77 Active
Deepest Floor: 93. Status: Active. They live streamed their descent past Sage's Solitude and are training for another push into the final stretch.
Deepest Floor: 90. Status: Retired. Several members took consulting positions at Monsera University after their last narrow escape.
Deepest Floor: 87. Status: Active. An unorthodox party known for treating deep dungeon delving like a high-stakes business venture.

Deepest Floor: 85 or deeper. Status: Unknown. The party checked in at Sage's Solitude and went on past it. They do not live stream, so no one knows how far they have gone. No one will know until they fall and show up in the locker area, or walk back out on their own.
Deepest Floor: 85. Status: Active. A mixed-heritage team from the port city of Breakwater.
Deepest Floor: 82. Status: Disbanded. Former members now run elite training camps in the upper safe zones.
Deepest Floor: 77. Status: Active. A young, hyper-aggressive party climbing the board quickly through high-risk strategies.

Building a character is a series of meaningful choices that together define who your character is, what they are good at, what they struggle with, and what keeps them going when things get difficult. The choices interact in ways that reward thought without requiring optimization. Start with the character that interests you, and everything else follows from that.

Character creation follows these thirteen steps in order. Each step points to the chapter that covers it in full. Step 1. Pick your Trope: Choose one Trope, the personality archetype at the heart of your character. Every Trope has a Boon and a Bane. The Boon gives you one bonus die on rolls with an ability tied to the Trope. The Bane gives you one penalty die on rolls with a fixed ability. Record your Trope at the top of your sheet. The full list is in Chapter 7 . Step 2. Consult the Scales: Your sheet has seven Virtue and Vice scales: Humility and Pride, Charity and Greed, Chastity and Lust, Patience and Wrath, Temperance and Gluttony, Kindness and Envy, and Diligence and Sloth. Mark where your character sits on each one: Two highs: two scales at High Virtue or High Vice, the 2 at either end. Two lows: two scales at Low Virtue or Low Vice, the 1 on either side. Three central: the other three scales stay at Central, the 0 in the middle. Then choose two Driving Factors, one for each of your highs. A Driving Factor is what your character wants, and it must match the scale and the side its high sits on. Your highs also set your starting Willpower in Step 9. The scales and every Driving Factor are covered in Chapter 7 , Part 2. Step 3. Assign your Role: Your Role is your position on the battlefield: a line (Frontline, Midline, or Backline) followed by one word for how you fight, such as Frontline Tank, Frontline Fighter, Midline Healer, Midline Support, Backline Mage, or Backline Rogue. Your Role decides where you start when combat begins. You can change it as play goes on if you want to try a different line of attack. Step 4. Choose your Heritage: Pick your heritage from Chapter 8 and record what it gives you: your Innate Attribute (it starts at 2 dots; note Innate beside it), your Innate Flaw, your Attribute Flaw, your Heritage Merit, and your free Heritage magic dot. Rare heritages need Storyteller approval. Step 5. Allocate your Attributes: Every attribute starts at 1 dot. Give each column (Physical, Social, and Mental) one of three designations, and write its number in the space next to the column's name on your sheet: Affinity: write 6. Standard: write 5. Aversion: write 4. That number is the column's cap, and it is also how many dots you spend across that column's three attributes. Your Attribute Flaw column can never be your Affinity. No attribute can be filled above 5 at creation. A Hyuman with Hyuman Adaptability writes 5 next to all three columns instead. Your Physical and Mental designations also set your dots in Steps 10 and 11. Step 6. Prioritize your Abilities: Abilities start at 0 dots. Give each of the six ability groups a different number from 2 to 7 and write it next to the group's name on your sheet. That number is how many dots you spend in that group, and no ability can be filled above 5 at creation. Any ability with 4 or more dots gets one free specialty: write a condition beside it, such as Awareness: Scent, for a bonus die when a roll fits. Then choose your Past Life Occupation, what your character did before arriving in Terrana, and write PL next to the abilities tied to it. Step 7. Select your Merits and Flaws: You have 7 points to spend on Merits. Each Flaw point you take gives you 1 more point, up to 7 more, for a maximum of 14. Record them in the Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section, along with your Heritage Merit. The full lists are in Chapter 9 . Step 8. Determine your Backgrounds: You have 7 points to spend on Backgrounds, plus any points left over from Step 7. Record them in the same section. Backgrounds are listed in Chapter 10 . Step 9. Set Willpower, Fate, and Sanity: Fill in 5 dots of each. If both of your highs are Vices, fill in only 4 dots of Willpower. If both are Virtues, fill in 6. One of each leaves it at 5. Fate and Sanity can only be changed at creation by Merits and Flaws ( Chapter 9 ). All three are covered in full in Chapter 11 . Step 10. Choose your Combat Styles: Your Physical column decides how many dots you spend on Combat Styles: 7 for Affinity, 5 for Standard, or 3 for Aversion. Spread them across any styles you like, up to 5 dots in one style, and mark each style with a P for Primary. Each dot unlocks that rank's Default Ability, plus your choice of its Option A or Option B ( Chapter 12 ). Step 11. Choose your Magical Knowledges: Your Mental column decides how many dots you spend on Magical Knowledges (casting schools, circle magic, and Battle Aura): 7 for Affinity, 5 for Standard, or 3 for Aversion, up to 5 dots in one knowledge. Mark each with a P for Primary. Your free Heritage magic dot from Step 4 is written here too, also marked with a P, and does not use these dots. For a casting school, each dot lets you choose one of that rank's two spells ( Chapter 13 ). Step 12. Spend your Freebie Points: You have 7 Freebie Points, though the Storyteller may adjust this. Mana starts at 1 dot, and this is the only time it can be raised during creation. Each dot costs: Attribute: 3 points. Ability: 2 points. Combat Style or Magical Knowledge: 4 points. A new style or knowledge bought here is marked with an S for Secondary. Background: 1 point. Mana: 7 points. Freebies cannot be spent on Merits, Flaws, Willpower, Fate, Sanity, or Heritage traits, and the Golden Rule still applies. Step 13. Calculate your Level: Add up all your dots in Attributes (including Mana), Abilities, Combat Styles, Magical Knowledges (including Heritage magic), and Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds. Write the total in the Level box. Willpower, Fate, Sanity, and Virtues and Vices do not count.

At character creation, nothing on your sheet may be filled in above 5 dots, not even with Freebie Points, no matter what modifier, bonus, or heritage benefit applies. There are no exceptions, including your Innate Attribute.

Attributes are organized into three groups, called columns: Physical, Social, and Mental. Each column contains three attributes. Physical Social Mental Strength Charisma Intelligence Dexterity Manipulation Perception Fortitude Composure Wisdom

Your Innate Attribute's maximum is 1 higher than its column's cap. P and S Markers: Only styles and knowledges taken in Steps 10 and 11, plus your free Heritage magic dot, get a P for Primary. Your thresholds decide what kind of damage an incoming attack or damage source does. Bashing Damage Threshold (BDT): Fortitude + Armor. Lethal Damage Threshold (LDT): BDT x2. Aggravated Damage Threshold (ADT): BDT x3.

If every ability in a group is filled to its current maximum, that group's maximum permanently rises by 1.

A specialty is a condition, written next to an ability, that gives you a bonus die when a roll fits it (for example, Awareness: Scent). Each ability can have up to 3 specialties. Any ability with 4 or more dots at character creation gets one free specialty. Every other specialty costs 5 XP and needs Storyteller approval.

Choose your character's Past Life Occupation: what they did, or loved doing, before they arrived in Terrana. It does not have to match the player's own life. Write PL next to each ability tied to that profession or hobby. Raising a PL ability costs the new dot x2 in XP, one less than a normal ability. That is the only benefit.

Everything in Terrana has some access to mana. Mana is rated from 1 to 10 dots, the only trait with ten. Every character starts with 1 dot. At creation, Mana can only be raised with Freebie Points, at 7 points per dot. After creation, each dot costs the new dot x7 in XP. Mana Pool: (Magic dots + Circle Magic dots) x Mana. Some items in the world let you add other abilities, such as Alchemy, Attunement, or Implements, but at creation and in most cases the pool uses only those two abilities. Maximum Mana Per Turn: Fortitude + Mana. This is the most mana you can safely spend in a single turn, no matter how large your pool is. How mana recovers, and everything else about Mana, Willpower, Fate, and Sanity, is covered in Chapter 11 .

At the end of each chapter of the story, every player earns XP: 1 XP for free, just for playing. 1 XP for acting: playing your character in the scene. 1 XP for answering a question the Storyteller asks, or for sharing something you learned that chapter. 1 bonus XP from your Affinity column, if you earned it (see below). Physical Affinity: Earn the bonus if your character took part in combat or made a big physical gesture during the chapter. Mental Affinity: Earn the bonus if your character used magic, or made a profound discovery or had a profound idea, during the chapter. Social Affinity: Earn the bonus automatically, as long as your character took part in the chapter in any way. If everyone at the table earned a bonus XP that chapter, you earn one more, for a total of 2 bonus XP.

Every character in this game is a person first and a set of numbers second. Before you touch your dice pools or dot allocations, you need to know who you are playing. Tropes and Driving Factors are the two pieces of your character that answer that question most directly. Your Trope is your personality in shorthand. Your Virtues and Vices are your values, set on seven scales. Your Driving Factors are your reasons for getting out of bed, and they come from the strongest of those values. Together they are the lens through which every mechanical choice you make should be viewed. The fighter who chose Battle Maniac and High Wrath is a fundamentally different person from the fighter who chose Reluctant Hero and High Patience, even if their dots end up looking similar on paper. None of this constrains your character; it gives them shape. You pick one Trope in Step 1 of character creation (Part 1 of this chapter). In Step 2 you set your seven scales and choose two Driving Factors, one for each of your highs (Part 2).

A Trope is a recognizable personality archetype, the kind that anyone who has watched enough anime or read enough light novels will identify immediately. They are not stereotypes; they are starting points. You do not have to choose a Trope from this list. If your character's personality does not map cleanly to any of these, work with your Storyteller to create something that fits. The list is a resource, not a rulebook. Each Trope provides a Boon and a Bane. Note them in the specialty field next to the relevant abilities on your sheet. The Boon: One bonus die on rolls with the chosen ability within the Trope's category. It stacks with any specialty already on that ability. The Bane: One penalty die on rolls with the fixed ability the Trope names. Virtues and Vices: Your scale positions also add or remove dice, depending on whether you are acting with or against them: 1 die at a low, 2 dice at a high. These stack with your Boon or Bane when both apply. This is why the scales on your sheet are marked 2, 1, 0, 1, 2. The Tropes are grouped by their Boon: each ability group has its own table, with two Tropes for every ability, in the same order as on your character sheet. A few more Tropes follow in Extra Tropes.
