At home at the helm of anything that flies. Precise and methodical, clumsy when improvisation is required. Pilot Acrobatics 38 Speed Demon Lives for the open road and the next faster ride. Too busy chasing the horizon to read the people around them. Pilot Insight 39 Wanderer No fixed home. Collects experiences instead of things. Has never learned to pilot a ship or any other vehicle. Ride Pilot 40 Feral One Raised outside civilization or close enough to it. Rides beasts as easily as walking. Hopeless at the controls of any ship or vehicle. Ride Pilot

# Trope Description Boon Bane 41 Full Metal Methodical and precise. Every transmutation deliberate. Quick sleight is not in their vocabulary. Alchemy Sleight of Hand 42 Mad Scientist Brilliant, obsessive, ethically flexible. Too chaotic to properly attune to magical items. Alchemy Attunement 43 Magical Bloodline Power runs in the family, for better or worse. Feels magic in the blood but never studied how to brew or refine it. Attunement Alchemy 44 Fey Chosen Marked by the fey and touched by something not quite of this world. Machines and vehicles never behave around them. Attunement Pilot 45 Arcanist Consumed by magical theory and the drawing of circles. Cannot always translate knowledge into instinctive physical action. Circle Magic Ranged 46 Bookworm Knows every circle and formula in theory. Struggles when theory meets reality at speed. Circle Magic Acrobatics 47 Shut-In Exceptional with gadgets and tools made at home. No wilderness instincts outside controlled environments. Implements Survival 48 Broken Ace Exceptional with every tool and implement. Held together with willpower and spite. Has stopped taking care of themselves. Implements Survival 49 Hedge Mage Self-taught, unconventional, effective in ways formal training cannot explain. Never learned the foundations. Magic Alchemy 50 Prodigy Naturally gifted with magic beyond reason. So focused on mastery they stop noticing what is happening around them. Magic Awareness

# Trope Description Boon Bane 51 Collector Obsessed with rare and valuable items. Everything is a potential addition to the collection. Artifacts Athletics 52 Opportunist Spots the angle and the value of a thing before anyone else sees the room. So transactional they burn bridges they could have invested in. Artifacts Commerce 53 Perfectionist Cannot submit work they consider unfinished. Rushed or imperfect conditions trigger a breakdown. Awareness Crafts 54 Stoic Veteran Has seen too much. Feels too little on the surface, and misses nothing. Too direct and practical for complex magical theory. Awareness Circle Magic 55 Artisan Obsessed with making things perfectly. Steady hands built for craft, not quick dexterous tricks. Crafts Sleight of Hand 56 Lore Keeper Devoted to preserving history and restoring ancient craft. Reveres artifacts too much to study them practically. Crafts Artifacts 57 Empath Feels everything everyone around them feels. A gift and a burden in equal measure. Insight Performance 58 Conspiracy Theorist Sees patterns and motives everywhere. Sometimes correct. Focused so hard on hidden meanings they miss what is in front of them. Insight Artifacts 59 Caretaker Puts everyone else first. Neglects their own creative projects entirely. Survival Crafts 60 Naturalist Deeply in tune with the living world and at home in the wild. Uncomfortable with manufactured magic and constructed items. Survival Implements

# Trope Description Boon Bane 61 Nihilist Nothing matters so why not try everything. Surprisingly effective. Deeply concerning. Endurance Melee 62 Tsundere Hostile on the surface, soft underneath. Swings first to hide genuine care. Melee Expression 63 Glass Cannon Hits like a freight train, folds like paper. Offense is everything, defense is someone else's problem. Martial Arts Endurance 64 Veteran Adventurer Has seen it all. Bored by almost everything. Relies on hard-won experience in the wild over magical theory. Survival Magic 65 Schemer Always three steps ahead. So focused on their own plans they miss nuance in others. Subterfuge Insight 66 Burnout Was exceptional once. Still is. Just exhausted. Has stopped paying attention to subtlety in people. Awareness Insight

s: Part 2: Virtues, Vices, and the Seven Scales
t: People are not consistent. They have values they hold deeply and impulses they struggle to control. They have principles they uphold under pressure and principles they abandon when the cost gets high enough. The Seven Scales put all of that on the table and make it mechanical. The scales do not tell you who your character is. They reflect who your character is right now, and they change as your character changes. A deeply compassionate person can, through choices made across sessions and arcs, shift toward something darker. A dangerously self-serving one can find their way toward something better. The scales move because people move.

Each scale runs between a Virtue and a Vice. Neither end is simply good or bad. They are two orientations toward the same human experience, and either can produce heroism or destruction depending on who carries it and why. Each scale has five positions, marked 2, 1, 0, 1, 2 on your sheet. The number is how many dice the position adds to rolls that fit it, and removes from rolls that go against it.

Position Mark Effect High Virtue 2 +2 dice on rolls that align with this Virtue. -2 dice when you try to act against it. Low Virtue 1 +1 die on rolls that align with this Virtue. -1 die when you try to act against it. Central 0 No bonus and no drawback. You are balanced on this scale. Low Vice 1 +1 die on rolls that align with this Vice. -1 die when you try to act against it. High Vice 2 +2 dice on rolls that align with this Vice. -2 dice when you try to act against it. These dice only apply when the scale genuinely matters to what your character is doing. A character at High Humility does not get bonus dice on every social roll, only when acting with real humility: deferring to others, admitting limits, putting someone else's needs ahead of their own recognition. The Storyteller decides when a scale is relevant. Scale dice stack with your Trope's Boon or Bane when both apply.

At character creation (Step 2), set your seven scales: Two highs: two scales at High Virtue or High Vice. Two lows: two scales at Low Virtue or Low Vice. Three central: the other three scales stay at Central. Then choose two Driving Factors, one for each of your highs, matching the scale and the side the high sits on. Every drive is listed with its scale in the Full Reference at the end of this chapter. The names are starting points: what matters is what your drive is at its core, and which scale and side it belongs to. If you have a custom drive in mind, work with your Storyteller to place it. Your highs also set your starting Willpower: both Vices start you at 4, both Virtues at 6, and one of each at 5. This only applies at creation. Once play begins, moving on the scales never changes your Willpower rating. Central scales are not inert. They are simply waiting.

Before committing to a significant action, players are encouraged to consult the scales: look at where your character sits on each relevant scale and let that shape how they weigh the choice. Consulting the scales is a roleplay tool first and a mechanical tool second. A character at High Patience thinking about charging into a fight does not need a roll to know that charging runs against who they are right now. They can feel it. Consulting the scales makes that feeling explicit at the table. The Storyteller may ask how your character is weighing the decision. What does their position tell them to do? What does the situation seem to demand? Are those the same thing? The answer is where interesting roleplay lives. A character never has to act in line with their scales. People struggle, slip, and sometimes act against their own values. But they should know when they are doing it, and so should the player.

A Virtue or Vice roll can come up in any situation where a character's position on a scale genuinely matters: combat, social encounters, exploration, or quiet moments between scenes. The Storyteller decides when a roll is called for. The most common triggers are: Temptation: a test or temptation that directly engages the character's position on a scale. Acting against: the character tries to act against their current position on a relevant scale. Acting with: the character acts in strong alignment with their position. The bonus dice simply apply, with no extra roll. A deliberate choice: the Storyteller presents a decision meant to engage one or more scales, and the character's choice decides whether their position helps or hinders them. Actions are the main trigger. Words count as actions, physical deeds count, and deliberately doing nothing when action was possible counts too, especially on scales like Diligence and Patience where inaction is itself a choice. When a roll is called for, the Storyteller names the scale and whether you are rolling with or against your position, and you add or remove dice accordingly. Success usually means the character can act without betraying their principles. Failure usually means Willpower or Sanity damage, depending on how serious the violation is.
When a character acts against their position on a scale, the cost depends on how serious the violation is and how strongly they hold that position.

Position Minor Violation Severe Violation High Virtue or High Vice 1 Willpower damage 1 or more Sanity damage, at the Storyteller's discretion Low Virtue or Low Vice 1 Willpower damage 1 Willpower damage. Never causes Sanity damage. Central No consequence No consequence Lows can only ever cost Willpower, no matter how serious the violation. The character feels the tension, but it does not break them. Highs cost more, because the character's identity is built around them. Acting against a high is not just a bad decision; it is a betrayal of something the character has built their sense of self around. A character at High Humility who publicly boasts about their achievements is acting against the deepest part of who they are right now. A character at High Pride forced to grovel, genuinely submitting rather than putting on a show, suffers the same way. Taking quiet pride in being humble is fine. It is the act of boasting that triggers the cost, not the feeling.

The scales move in response to the choices made in play. The Storyteller tracks shifts and announces them. When a choice warrants a shift, the Storyteller tells the player right away that their scales have shifted. How far the dot moves is revealed at the end of the story chapter, giving the player time to reflect on what led to it before the sheet changes. Most shifts move a dot one position. A dramatic choice can move it as far as the Storyteller judges fitting, even across the center or from one end of the scale to the other. How far it moves depends on the action and how big a violation of the character's position it was. The size of the action sets the size of the shift. A character at High Lust who turns down someone they have no interest in triggers nothing. The same character who genuinely wants someone and refuses, again and again, to act on it, denying their nature rather than being patient, may find their dot drifting toward Central or beyond. Every shift, in either direction, does damage. Small shifts cause Willpower damage; significant shifts cause Sanity damage. A character's sense of self is shaken when their values move, even toward something better. Change is costly. Shifts never change the character's Willpower rating itself.

Your Driving Factors are tied to your highs. If a high shifts away from its end of the scale, you lose that Drive. It is no longer what gets you out of bed in the morning. If any other scale shifts all the way to a high, you gain a new Drive. The Storyteller assigns it based on the choices that caused the shift and which end you moved toward. It is not the player's choice in the moment; the Storyteller responds to what the character actually did across the arc. There is no limit: a character can have as many Drives as they have highs. A character who begins play driven by Compassion and ends a long campaign driven by something much darker has not failed. They have changed, and the system makes that change visible. If a player disagrees with how their scales shifted, or with the Drive assigned to a new high, they should say so. The Storyteller has the final say but should listen to the player's view of their own character. If the disagreement holds, the table reviews the specific choices together. The scales work best when everyone agrees on what they mean.

Rael sits at High Patience, driven by Steadfast. His party faces mercenaries who have cornered a group of civilians, and one of them taunts Rael, calling him a coward for holding back. Charging in to silence the taunt would go against his position, and the Storyteller reminds the player that Rael would take 2 penalty dice to do it. The player has Rael hold his ground, absorb the taunt, and wait for the right moment. Because he is acting in line with his scale, no roll is needed, and his 2 bonus dice apply to his next coordinated action with the party.

Mirren is Central on Kindness and Envy. A rival has just received an honor she wanted. The Storyteller calls for no roll: she has no strong orientation to act with or against, so she can feel and respond however she likes without mechanical consequence.

Davan is at High Charity, driven by Generosity. Across an arc he made several choices that put his own gain ahead of others, justifying each in the moment. At the end of the arc the Storyteller tells him his scales have shifted: his Charity and Greed dot has moved from High Charity to Central. He loses Generosity and takes Sanity damage. The player and Storyteller agree the move reflects what happened in the story.

Saya began play Central on Patience and Wrath. Over two arcs she kept choosing confrontation and meeting injustice with force. At the end of the second arc the Storyteller moves her to High Wrath and assigns her a new Drive, Righteous, because her anger was always aimed at things that deserved it. She takes Sanity damage, and she now has three Drives.

The Storyteller shifts a character two positions toward High Pride after a session where they publicly celebrated a victory. The player disagrees: the celebration felt earned. The table walks through the moments the Storyteller flagged and agrees the celebration was fine, but that brushing off a teammate's contribution was the real trigger. The shift is reduced to one position, and the game goes on.

Each scale below describes what acting with or against each position tends to look like, followed by the Driving Factors that belong to it. These are guides to what each scale is about, not a complete list of triggers.

Scale Core Tension Humility / Pride Where do I place my own worth relative to others? Charity / Greed Do I give or do I keep? Chastity / Lust Do I restrain or do I pursue? Patience / Wrath Do I endure or do I act on my anger? Temperance / Gluttony Do I hold back or do I commit fully? Kindness / Envy Do I care for others or do I want what they have? Diligence / Sloth Do I work or do I rest?

This scale governs the character's relationship with their own worth and the worth of others. Humility is the orientation of recognizing limitations and the value of others. Pride is the orientation of asserting worth, standing, and superiority. Position Acting In Accordance Acting Against High Humility (2) Deferring to others, acknowledging mistakes without defensiveness, placing others' recognition above your own, serving something greater than yourself Boasting, claiming credit, dismissing others' contributions, positioning yourself as superior Low Humility (1) Generally modest behavior, avoiding unnecessary self-promotion, crediting others when appropriate Consistent pattern of self-aggrandizement or dismissing others Central (0) No strong orientation in either direction. Acts of both humility and pride are available without mechanical consequence N/A Low Pride (1) Asserting your own worth, maintaining your standing, refusing to be diminished without cause Consistent self-deprecation that undermines your own agency or capability High Pride (2) Demanding recognition, establishing dominance, refusing submission, asserting superiority in meaningful ways Genuinely submitting, accepting diminishment, deferring when your standing is directly challenged

Factor High Description Devotion Humility You exist to serve something greater than yourself. A person, a cause, a community. Their wellbeing is your measure of success. Selfless, outward focused. Penance Humility You believe you are less than others and spend your life trying to prove you deserve to exist. Self-destructive, inward focused. Honor Pride You carry a name, a people, or a standard and you will not let it fall. Everything you do reflects on something larger than yourself. Outward focused but driven by pride. Dominance Pride You need to be the best. Not respected, not admired. The best. Everyone else is competition. Purely self-serving.

This scale governs the character's relationship with resources, generosity, and accumulation. Charity is the orientation of giving and sharing. Greed is the orientation of acquiring and keeping. Position Acting In Accordance Acting Against High Charity (2) Giving freely at personal cost, sharing resources without expectation of return, prioritizing others' needs over personal accumulation Hoarding, refusing to share when sharing is possible, prioritizing personal gain at direct cost to others Low Charity (1) Generally generous behavior, sharing when it is not too costly, not prioritizing personal accumulation over others' clear needs Consistent pattern of selfishness or accumulation at others' expense Central (0) No strong orientation in either direction N/A Low Greed (1) Prioritizing personal resources, making acquisitions, being selective about what you give away Consistent pattern of giving away things that meaningfully diminish your own position High Greed (2) Acquiring for yourself, refusing to give up what is yours, placing personal accumulation above other considerations Genuine generosity that costs you something significant with no expectation of return

Factor High Description Generosity Charity You give freely and genuinely. What you have is meant to be shared. The wellbeing of others is worth more to you than anything you could keep. Selfless, outward focused. Patronage Charity You give, but giving is how you accumulate influence, loyalty, and power. Charity is your tool. Inward focused dressed in outward clothing. Ambition Greed You want more, but what you build will outlast you and provide for others whether you intended it or not. The drive is personal but the result is outward. Avarice Greed You accumulate for yourself alone. What is yours is yours. Everyone else can find their own. Purely self-serving.

This scale governs the character's relationship with desire, restraint, and pursuit. Chastity is the orientation of discipline and withholding. Lust is the orientation of desire and pursuit. Position Acting In Accordance Acting Against High Chastity (2) Consistent restraint, denying yourself things you genuinely want, maintaining discipline even when desire is strong Giving in to desire, pursuing what you want without restraint, abandoning discipline for immediate gratification Low Chastity (1) Generally restrained behavior, exercising discipline in most situations Consistent pattern of pursuing desires without meaningful restraint Central (0) No strong orientation in either direction N/A Low Lust (1) Pursuing what you want, acting on attraction and desire, prioritizing pleasure Consistent denial of desire that feels genuine rather than strategic High Lust (2) Actively pursuing whoever has captured your attention, acting on desire when it is present, refusing to deny what you want Genuine denial of desire for someone you have clearly expressed wanting, restraint that is not strategic but actual

Factor High Description Discipline Chastity You hold yourself to a standard because you believe who you are when no one is watching matters. Your restraint makes you dependable, trustworthy, present for others. Outward focused. Repression Chastity You deny yourself everything because wanting feels dangerous. Your restraint is a wall that keeps you safe and everyone else out. Inward, self-protective. Passion Lust You feel everything fully and it drives you to create, connect, and act with a courage that more restrained people cannot access. The fire burns for others as much as for yourself. Outward focused. Indulgence Lust You pursue what you want because you want it. Consequences are for people with less appetite. Purely self-serving.

This scale governs the character's relationship with anger, restraint under pressure, and the choice between waiting and acting. Patience is the orientation of endurance and calm. Wrath is the orientation of anger and confrontation. Position Acting In Accordance Acting Against High Patience (2) Holding back when action is tempting, absorbing provocation without response, being the steady presence when others are volatile Charging in, responding to provocation with force, letting anger drive action Low Patience (1) Generally measured behavior, not responding to every provocation Consistent pattern of impulsive or anger-driven action Central (0) No strong orientation in either direction N/A Low Wrath (1) Responding to provocation, not letting things go easily, acting on anger when it is present Consistent pattern of absorbing provocation without any response High Wrath (2) Acting on anger, confronting what deserves confrontation, refusing to make peace with things that should be opposed Genuinely letting things go, absorbing significant provocation without any response, choosing patience when your anger is directly engaged

Factor High Description Steadfast Patience You are the anchor. When everything is chaos you are calm, and that calm is a gift to everyone around you. You endure so others do not have to. Outward focused. Passivity Patience You endure because acting is harder than waiting. You mistake tolerance for wisdom and let things happen that you should have stopped. Inward, self-protective. Righteous Wrath Your anger is a weapon aimed at things that deserve to be opposed. You fight because someone has to and you refuse to make peace with injustice. Outward focused. Rage Wrath You are angry and the world will know it. What your anger costs others is not your concern. Purely self-serving.

This scale governs the character's relationship with moderation, excess, and commitment. Temperance is the orientation of balance and measured engagement. Gluttony is the orientation of total investment and consumption. Position Acting In Accordance Acting Against High Temperance (2) Measured engagement, refusing excess, maintaining balance even when full commitment is available Going all in, consuming without limit, committing fully when moderation was an option Low Temperance (1) Generally moderate behavior, avoiding obvious excess Consistent pattern of all-or-nothing engagement Central (0) No strong orientation in either direction N/A Low Gluttony (1) Committing fully when the opportunity is there, consuming what is available, going beyond moderation when the situation calls for it Consistent moderation when full commitment was possible and warranted High Gluttony (2) Total commitment, consuming fully, refusing to do anything halfway Holding back, choosing moderation, refusing to fully commit when the thing in front of you clearly demands everything you have

Factor High Description Balance Temperance You regulate yourself because a clear head and a steady hand serve the people around you better than any excess ever could. Your moderation is a gift to others. Outward focused. Restraint Temperance You hold back because committing fully feels dangerous. You never invest enough to get hurt and call it wisdom. Inward, self-protective. Obsession Gluttony You cannot do anything halfway. That total commitment burns bright and occasionally illuminates something extraordinary for everyone around you. Outward focused. Excess Gluttony You consume because you want more. What your appetite costs others is not something you lose sleep over. Purely self-serving.

This scale governs the character's relationship with care for others and desire for what others have. Kindness is the orientation of compassion and giving. Envy is the orientation of wanting and resenting. Position Acting In Accordance Acting Against High Kindness (2) Genuine care for others' wellbeing, acting to help even at personal cost, responding to suffering with action Ignoring others' suffering, prioritizing your own desires over clear need in others, sabotaging someone else's wellbeing Low Kindness (1) Generally caring behavior, helping when it is not too costly Consistent indifference to others' wellbeing Central (0) No strong orientation in either direction N/A Low Envy (1) Wanting what others have, feeling the pull of comparison, pursuing what you see in others Consistent contentment with what you have when you clearly want more High Envy (2) Acting on the desire for what others have, letting comparison drive action, refusing to accept that someone else has something you want without pursuing it yourself Genuine contentment with what you have when someone you care about or compete with has something you want

Factor High Description Compassion Kindness You care for others because their suffering genuinely moves you. You give your time, your energy, and yourself freely because that is simply who you are. Outward focused. Codependence Kindness You give care because being needed is the only thing that makes you feel safe. Your kindness keeps people close for your sake as much as theirs. Inward, self-protective. Aspiration Envy You see what others have and it lights a fire under you. You want what they have badly enough to work for it, and that drive pushes you further than comfort ever would. Outward focused in outcome if not in origin. Resentment Envy You want what others have and cannot stand that they have it. Your envy poisons your relationships and makes the world feel smaller. Purely self-serving and destructive.

This scale governs the character's relationship with effort, engagement, and rest. Diligence is the orientation of work and purpose. Sloth is the orientation of stillness and disengagement. Position Acting In Accordance Acting Against High Diligence (2) Working consistently, pushing through exhaustion, refusing to stop when something remains undone Choosing rest when work remains, delegating when you should do it yourself, stopping before something is finished Low Diligence (1) Generally hardworking behavior, completing tasks reliably Consistent pattern of avoidance or incomplete follow-through Central (0) No strong orientation in either direction N/A Low Sloth (1) Taking your time, not pushing when rest is available, declining to engage when engagement is optional Consistent pattern of forcing yourself to work when rest was available and warranted High Sloth (2) Refusing to engage, taking rest when action is available, moving at your own pace regardless of external pressure Pushing yourself to work, committing to effort when disengagement was available, forcing engagement when you could have stepped back

Factor High Description Purpose Diligence You work because what you are building matters, to you and to the people it will serve when it is done. Your effort is directed outward and the results show it. Outward focused. Compulsion Diligence You work because stopping means feeling something you are not ready to feel. The work is for you, not for what it produces. Inward, self-protective. Stillness Sloth You move at your own pace because the world moves too fast to see clearly. Your unhurried perspective produces things that relentless effort never could. Outward focused in outcome. Apathy Sloth You do not engage because engaging is hard and the outcome probably does not matter anyway. The world can sort itself out. Purely self-serving.

From the preface to "Peoples of the Known World" by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University This book is a field survey of the peoples of Terrana, compiled over many years of travel for Monsera University. Each entry records what I observed, who I spoke with, and where my earlier assumptions proved wrong. Where I have not met a people myself, I say so. Where a people asked me to keep something private, I have. Every person in Terrana inherits things they did not choose: a lifespan, a body, a reputation, and often a small piece of magic carried in the blood. That inheritance is the subject of this book.

Your heritage partially shapes what you are naturally good at, what you carry with you that you did not choose, and how the world tends to see you before you have had a chance to make any impression of your own. Every heritage in this chapter gives your character the following. Choose your heritage at Step 4 of character creation and record each of them on your sheet. Innate Attribute: One attribute starts at 2 dots and has its maximum raised by 1 beyond the column cap. Note Innate next to it on your sheet. Most heritages offer two attributes to choose between. Hyumans and born Vampires may choose any attribute. Innate Flaw: The Innate Flaw is not chosen and grants no extra dots. It is simply part of who your character is. Attribute Flaw: Every heritage except Hyumans and Vampires is naturally weaker in one attribute group: Physical, Social, or Mental. That group can never be your Affinity column; it can only be your Standard or Aversion column. This is separate from your Innate Flaw, and Merits can still raise attributes in the flawed group. Heritage Merit: Choose one of the merits listed for your heritage and record it in your Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section. You only receive a free dot if the merit itself says so. Heritage Magic: Every character begins with 1 free dot in the Heritage magic of their heritage. The rules for Heritage magic follow below. Lifespan: Every heritage has one of four lifespans: 100, 200, 400, or 1000 years. A few are Immortal, meaning no one truly knows how long they live, such as slimes, vampires, and the Immortal Demon Kings.

Heritages are divided into Common and Rare based on how many of them live across Terrana and how often the rest of the world encounters them. Common Heritages are available to every player. Choosing a Rare Heritage makes your character an unusual sight almost everywhere they go, and it requires Storyteller approval before character creation begins.

Long before anyone in Terrana studies a school of magic, most of them already know a little of it. A Beastfolk child howls and the birds scatter. A Dwarven apprentice lays a hand on a cracked ingot and feels where the flaw runs. Nobody taught them. The magic was in the blood, waiting. Heritage magic is that inheritance. It is a discipline of its own, separate from the seven casting schools of the heptagram and separate from Battle Aura. It has no school color and no place on the Mages Guild star. It is not learned in a classroom. It wakes up. Every technique in a Heritage magic is a spell, follows the same rules as any other spell, and costs mana.

Every character begins with 1 free dot in the Heritage magic their heritage provides. Record it in the Magical Knowledges section of your sheet. Any character may instead give up that free dot and take 1 dot in any casting school (Fire, Water, Air, Earth, Nature, Bright, or Shade) or any circle magic. This is a permanent choice. The character can still raise their Heritage magic later with XP, starting from zero. Either way, a character receives only one free dot. Freebie points cannot be spent on Heritage magic.

Heritage magic is rated from 1 to 7 and uses the same rank names as every other magic. 1 Core 2 Terrestrial 3 Aerial 4 Lunar 5 Stellar 6 Galactic 7 Cosmic Raising Heritage magic costs XP equal to the new dot x5, the same as a Magical Knowledge. Each new dot also requires an Awakening: a moment in the story where the bloodline stirs. A near death experience, a meeting with an elder of your people, a choice that echoes your ancestors. The Storyteller approves the Awakening, and it can happen during a session or between them.

Every rank offers two spells, Option A and Option B. Each time you gain a dot, choose one of that rank's two spells. The choice is permanent. The spell you did not choose can never be learned, with XP or any other way. Hyumans are the one exception (see Adaptation). Two characters of the same heritage can carry the same bloodline and still express it very differently.

Every spell is written out in the same format. Mana Cost: What the spell costs. Every Heritage magic spell costs mana equal to its rank: 1 at Core, 2 at Terrestrial, and so on up to 7 at Cosmic. Speed: Instant spells take effect on your action. Reaction spells are cast in response to something that happens outside your turn. Extended spells keep working after they are cast. Downtime spells can only be cast outside combat. Type: What the spell does: Attack, Defense, Debuff, Enhancement, Healing, Movement, Utility, or Conjuration. Persistent, Attuned, or Countdown is added when the spell lasts. Range: Who or what the spell can affect. Dice Pool: What you roll. "None" means the spell takes effect without a roll. Defense: What the target rolls against the spell. "Target's choice of defense" means the target defends against the attack however they normally would. A named pool, such as Composure + Insight, means the target rolls that pool against your successes and the spell only takes hold if you rolled more. "None" means nothing rolls against it. Use: Whether the spell works in combat, outside combat, or both. Effect: Exactly what happens.

A Heritage magic dice pool is Attribute + Ability + Heritage dots. Each Heritage magic lists a Primary pool and a Secondary pool, and each spell says which one it uses. Heritage dots always means your dots in the Heritage magic the spell belongs to. You may spend extra mana beyond a spell's cost to add 1 die per mana, declared before rolling, up to your Heritage dots or Max Mana Per Turn, whichever comes first. This limit applies any time you spend mana to boost a spell, including spells whose damage value is set by successes plus mana spent. Each Heritage magic has one fixed mana assignment that says whether that extra mana can go to the attack roll, the damage roll, or either. Unless a spell says otherwise, an Attack spell resolves like any magic attack. The target chooses their own defense, and a hit carries into the damage roll as normal. When a spell says a target resists, they roll the listed pool against your successes, and the spell only takes hold if you rolled more. When a spell lets you resist something with magic, such as being knocked down or moved, you spend the spell's mana and roll the dice pool it names. Your Heritage dots are already part of that pool.

Some spells last beyond the moment they are cast. They work in one of three ways. Persistent: Pay the mana cost to cast it. To keep it running, pay upkeep during each Upkeep Phase. Upkeep is always the spell's mana cost minus 1, so a Core spell costs nothing to maintain and a Cosmic spell costs 6. Stop paying and it ends. Outside combat, a Persistent spell lasts one scene for its casting cost. Attuned: Attuned spells work like attuning to an item. Pay the mana cost from your Max Mana Per Turn and leave it there, committed to the spell. The spell stays active as long as that mana stays committed, and that mana cannot be used for anything else in the meantime. You may end an Attuned spell at any time, and the committed mana returns to your Max Mana Per Turn. Use the Committed track on your combat mat to keep count. Countdown: Countdown spells hold a target for a limited time. Pay the mana cost to cast it, adding extra mana if you wish. The spell lasts a number of turns equal to half the total mana spent on it, rounded up. One turn comes off the countdown during each Upkeep Phase. During any Upkeep Phase you may pay the spell's cost minus 1 to freeze the countdown, so that turn does not come off. The spell ends when the countdown runs out or when the ending condition in its Effect happens, whichever comes first. Outside combat, a Countdown spell lasts one scene for its casting cost, like a Persistent spell, unless its ending condition happens first.

A Conjuration spell creates something that acts on its own: an awakened tree, an imagined creature, a risen body. A conjuration is always Persistent. It has no Health track and no character sheet of its own. During each Upkeep Phase, after its upkeep is paid, it may take the action its spell describes, rolling your dice pool for that spell. A conjuration ends when its upkeep is not paid, when you are Incapacitated, or when another spell banishes it.

Heritage magic has no element. It never gains elemental advantage, never suffers elemental disadvantage, and never triggers elemental interactions with shields, walls, or summons. It cannot be used as part of combination magic. A character cannot learn another heritage's magic, with two exceptions. Mixed heritage characters may use either parent's Heritage magic, as described below. Contract Magic is a circle magic, and anyone may learn it, though devils are the only people born with it. Like every circle magic, it can only be written outside combat.

Terrana is old enough, and Monsera crowded enough, that plenty of people have parents of two different heritages. A mixed heritage character chooses one parent's heritage for their Innate Attribute, Innate Flaw, and Heritage Merit. For their free Heritage magic dot, they may choose the Heritage magic of either parent. Only one bloodline awakens. The other stays quiet.

A character with one Fey or devil parent and one parent of any other heritage is Fey Touched. They follow the Mixed Heritage rules above, with one addition: a Fey Touched character lives about 400 years, whatever their other parent's lifespan. A Fey Touched Hyuman can expect to see four centuries. Devil Spawn are Fey Touched.

All healing in Terrana, magical or otherwise, works in tiers. Each success on a healing roll does one of the things its tier allows, chosen by the healer. Slaking a box lowers it one damage type (Aggravated to Lethal, or Lethal to Bashing). Neutralizing a box removes it entirely. Basic healing: Each success neutralizes 1 Bashing, or slakes 1 Lethal to Bashing. Basic healing cannot affect Aggravated damage. Advanced healing: Each success neutralizes 2 Bashing, neutralizes 1 Lethal, or slakes 1 Aggravated to Lethal. Expert healing: Each success neutralizes 4 Bashing, neutralizes 2 Lethal, or neutralizes 1 Aggravated. Master healing: Regrows lost limbs. Master healing can never be used in combat; the incantation takes several turns to complete. It is rare. Automaton prosthetics are common across Terrana, and some people would rather replace a lost limb with a stronger one than regrow it. Resurrection: The only healing above Master. It has its own chapter. Aggravated damage healed during the same combat in which it was taken usually leaves no scar, and that healing can even reattach a severed limb that is still on hand.

A creature that falls rolls 1d10 for every 10 feet it falls. One zone straight up or down is about 10 feet. Falling damage is not a success roll: add the numbers shown on the dice, and that total is the damage. If the total is lower than the creature's BDT, it takes no damage. Otherwise it takes the damage like any other hit.

From "Peoples of the Known World" by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University Before the Slime King arrived, Monsera island was not a lawless wilderness of mindless creatures, as some accounts claim. It was home to many peoples who had not yet organized into a state an outsider would recognize. These monster peoples are the original inhabitants of Monsera and the Shaded Isles to its east. The current kingdom was built with them, not in spite of them. What follows is a short orientation to each group, not a full account. Each would need a volume of its own. The ten Monster sub-types listed here are broad categories. Players are encouraged to work with their Storyteller to define their specific creature type. The mechanical blocks below are starting points. With Storyteller approval a player may request adjustments. Monster lifespans vary by sub-type and are listed in each entry. Corporeal Undead are Immortal as long as they never fully deplete their mana for an extended period. Incorporeal Undead cannot be chosen at character creation. A character can only become one during play. Four Monster sub-types are Common Heritages and are listed alphabetically in this part, marked Monster Faction. The other six are Rare and appear in Part 2.

Aarakocra, Harpies, and similar. Avian monsters share some heritage with the Skyfolk in the broad sense that both have wings, but the similarities largely end there. From Liris Kant's entry on the monster peoples The Avian peoples, aarakocra, harpies, and other winged kin, are often compared to the Skyfolk. The comparison does not hold. Where Skyfolk are ancient, isolated, and detached, Avians are social, loud, and interested in everything happening around them. In Monsera they gather on rooftops, and several rooftop districts have become Avian neighborhoods by common agreement.

Average Lifespan: 200 years. Innate Attribute (choose 1, note Innate on sheet): Dexterity: For a character whose aerial agility and swift precise movement define them. Perception: For a character whose sharp eyesight and environmental awareness define them. Innate Flaw - Hollow Bones: Avian monsters suffer a penalty die on Endurance rolls against physical trauma. Their lighter build makes them faster in the air and more fragile on the ground. Attribute Flaw - Social: Social attributes cannot be your Affinity column. They can only be your Standard or Aversion column. Flight: Avian monsters fly naturally at double their normal movement without magic. Record a free specialty in Athletics called Flight, providing a bonus die on Athletics rolls made while flying. Heritage Merit (choose 1, record in Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section): Aerial Agility: Grants a free specialty in Acrobatics called Aerial Agility, providing a bonus die on rolls involving flight maneuvers, aerial combat, and movement in three dimensional space. Keen Eye: Grants a free specialty in Awareness called Keen Eye, providing a bonus die on sight based Awareness rolls including long distance observation and spotting hidden things.

The Avian peoples turned rooftops into neighborhoods and every gutter into a conversation. Skycall is wind and voice: the dive from above, the call that brings the flock, and the wingbeat that knocks enemies out of the air. Avian peoples fly naturally; Skycall makes them better at it. Primary: Dexterity + Acrobatics + Skycall Secondary: Charisma + Performance + Skycall Extra mana: Attack only. 1 die per mana, up to your Skycall dots or Max Mana Per Turn, whichever comes first.

Mana Cost: 1, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Movement, Attuned Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While attuned and flying, move one extra zone each turn at no AP cost.

Mana Cost: 1 Speed: Instant Type: Utility Use: Combat and outside combat Range: A settlement Dice Pool: Charisma + Performance + Skycall Defense: None Effect: A call heard across a settlement. Birds and avian kin who hear it answer one simple question per success about what they have seen.

Mana Cost: 2 Speed: Instant Type: Attack Use: Combat Range: Melee Dice Pool: Dexterity + Acrobatics + Skycall Defense: Target's choice of defense Effect: Attack after descending at least one zone this turn. Add your Heritage dots to the damage roll.

Mana Cost: 2 Speed: Instant Type: Debuff Use: Combat Range: One target in an adjacent zone Dice Pool: Dexterity + Acrobatics + Skycall Defense: Perception + Awareness Effect: The target resists with Perception + Awareness. If you beat them, they suffer -2 dice on sight-based rolls on their next turn.
Mana Cost: 3 Speed: Reaction Type: Movement Use: Combat Range: One ally in an adjacent zone Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: Move the ally one zone at no AP cost to them.

Mana Cost: 3 Speed: Instant Type: Debuff Use: Combat Range: All adjacent zones Dice Pool: Charisma + Performance + Skycall Defense: Composure + Presence Effect: Every enemy in range resists with Composure + Presence. Each one you beat loses their next Reaction.

Mana Cost: 4, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Defense, Attuned Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While attuned and flying, you ignore Difficult Terrain, and melee attackers without reach or flight suffer -2 dice against you.

Mana Cost: 4, upkeep 3 each Upkeep Phase Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Debuff, Persistent Use: Combat Range: One zone in sight Dice Pool: Charisma + Performance + Skycall Defense: None Effect: A swarm of birds fills the zone. While maintained, enemies there suffer -2 dice on all rolls.

Mana Cost: 5 Speed: Instant Type: Utility Use: Combat Range: One target in an adjacent zone Dice Pool: Dexterity + Acrobatics + Skycall Defense: Strength + Athletics Effect: The target resists with Strength + Athletics. If you beat them, choose one: carry them up to two zones, fly them up to two zones straight up, or carry them one zone and fly them one zone straight up. Then drop them. They take damage equal to your Heritage dots, plus falling damage if they fall (see Falling Damage).

Mana Cost: 5, upkeep 4 each Upkeep Phase Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Enhancement, Persistent Use: Combat Range: Allies in sight who can hear you Dice Pool: Charisma + Performance + Skycall Defense: None Effect: While maintained, allies who can hear you add bonus dice equal to half your Heritage dots, rounded up, to Dodge rolls.

Mana Cost: 6 Speed: Instant Type: Attack Use: Combat Range: A straight line up to four zones Dice Pool: Dexterity + Acrobatics + Skycall Defense: Target's choice of defense Effect: Fly along the line, ending in an empty zone. Roll once; each enemy along the line defends separately.

Mana Cost: 6, upkeep 5 each Upkeep Phase Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Debuff, Persistent Use: Combat Range: All adjacent zones Dice Pool: Dexterity + Acrobatics + Skycall Defense: Dexterity + Acrobatics Effect: Roll when cast. While maintained, ranged attacks through those zones suffer -3 dice, and flying enemies there must beat your successes with Dexterity + Acrobatics during each Upkeep Phase or fall and take falling damage (see Falling Damage).

Mana Cost: 7, upkeep 6 each Upkeep Phase Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Movement, Persistent Use: Combat and outside combat Range: Self and allies in sight Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While maintained, you and allies in sight move one extra zone each turn at no AP cost, and allies can fly at double their normal movement.

s: B. Call of a Thousand Wings
t: Mana Cost: 7, upkeep 6 each Upkeep Phase Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Debuff, Persistent Use: Combat Range: Up to 6 connected zones in sight Dice Pool: Charisma + Performance + Skycall Defense: None Effect: While maintained, enemies in those zones suffer -3 dice on all rolls, and allies there count as fully covered against ranged attacks.

From "Peoples of the Known World" by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University The Beastfolk are native to the Great Forest on the Milis Continent. Individuals live in Monsera, Breakwater, and other cities, but in small numbers. The exception is the Holy Kingdom of Milishion on the forest's edge, where Beastfolk make up about a quarter of the population. No other nation comes close. Their settlements are built high in the trees. These are full communities with streets, gathering places, and homes expanded over generations. Contact with Monsera has brought better lighting, crystal relay access, and improved building materials. The Beastfolk adopted what was useful and declined the rest. Each tribe has its own chief, and all chiefs answer to a head chief. By law and tradition, the head chief must come from a canine or feline bloodline. The Doldia family has held the position for generations. The other chiefs can jointly demand that the head chief step down, and the head chief may demand a formal challenge before stepping aside. Tribes differ in temperament. Some settle disputes quickly and loudly. Others are slow to anger and slow to forgive. All share a strong territorial sense. They protect the forest out of obligation, not hostility toward outsiders. Breeding seasons vary by animal type and are treated as a private matter. Rabbit Beastfolk are the only type broadly known to seek companionship outside their season. I include this because people ask, and an accurate answer is better than a guess. Splashing water on a Beastfolk person is one of the worst insults in their culture, and the response is usually physical. Visitors should know this before it happens by accident.

Average Lifespan: 100 years. Innate Attribute (choose 1, note Innate on sheet): Perception: For a character whose sharp natural senses and awareness define them. Dexterity: For a character whose physical agility and predatory grace define them. Innate Flaw - Animalistic Instincts: Every Beastfolk character has an innate flaw derived from the animal type they most closely resemble. Work with your Storyteller to define a specific instinctive weakness that fits your animal heritage. The flaw should create a meaningful penalty die in situations where that instinct would work against the character. Attribute Flaw - Mental: Mental attributes cannot be your Affinity column. They can only be your Standard or Aversion column. Heritage Merit (choose 1, record in Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section): Pack Sense: Grants a free specialty in Awareness called Pack Sense. While at least one ally occupies a zone adjacent to yours, touching it directly or diagonally, you also gain a bonus die on attack rolls. Predator's Instinct: Grants a free specialty in either Awareness or Athletics reflecting the character's natural hunting instincts and physical predatory capability.

Beastfolk blend mana into their voices. A trained howl can rattle bone, scatter a charge, or carry a warning through a whole forest. Howling Magic is loud, direct, and impossible to ignore. Primary: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Secondary: Perception + Awareness + Howling Magic Extra mana: Attack only. 1 die per mana, up to your Howling Magic dots or Max Mana Per Turn, whichever comes first.

Mana Cost: 1 Speed: Instant Type: Debuff Use: Combat Range: One target in an adjacent zone Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: Composure + Presence Effect: The target resists with Composure + Presence. If you beat them, they lose their next Reaction.

Mana Cost: 1, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Enhancement, Attuned Use: Combat and outside combat Range: Self Dice Pool: Perception + Awareness + Howling Magic Defense: None Effect: While attuned, add your Heritage dots to Awareness rolls based on hearing or scent.

Mana Cost: 2 Speed: Instant Type: Debuff Use: Combat Range: One target in sight Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: Composure + Presence Effect: The target resists with Composure + Presence. If you beat them, they suffer penalty dice on their next roll equal to your extra successes, up to your Heritage dots.

Mana Cost: 2 Speed: Instant Type: Utility Use: Combat and outside combat Range: A settlement or a few miles of open land Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: None Effect: A howl that carries a long way. Allies who hear it know your direction and whether you are in danger. Anyone else nearby may hear it too.

Mana Cost: 3 Speed: Instant Type: Debuff Use: Combat Range: All adjacent zones Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: Composure + Presence Effect: Every enemy in range resists with Composure + Presence. Each one you beat loses 1 AP on their next turn.

Mana Cost: 3, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Utility, Attuned Use: Combat and outside combat Range: Self Dice Pool: Perception + Awareness + Howling Magic Defense: Dexterity + Stealth Effect: While attuned, roll your dice pool whenever a hidden or invisible creature moves within a number of zones equal to your Howling Magic dots. The creature rolls Dexterity + Stealth. If you beat it, you know which zone it is in.

Mana Cost: 4 Speed: Instant Type: Attack Use: Combat Range: One target in sight Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: Fortitude + Endurance Effect: A sonic attack. The target defends with Fortitude + Endurance instead of Dodge.

Mana Cost: 4 Speed: Instant Type: Enhancement Use: Combat Range: Allies in sight who can hear you Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: None Effect: Each ally ends one fear or panic effect and adds a bonus die to their next attack.

Mana Cost: 5 Speed: Instant Type: Attack Use: Combat Range: Cone: all zones directly and diagonally forward of you Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: Fortitude + Endurance Effect: Shatterhowl against every target in the cone. Roll once; each target defends separately with Fortitude + Endurance.

Mana Cost: 5, upkeep 4 each Upkeep Phase Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Debuff, Persistent Use: Combat Range: All adjacent zones Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: Composure + Expression Effect: Roll when cast. While maintained, anyone other than you in range must beat your successes with Composure + Expression to cast spoken spells, Vocal Magic, or Howling Magic.

Mana Cost: 6 Speed: Instant Type: Debuff Use: Combat Range: All adjacent zones Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: Composure + Presence Effect: Every enemy in range resists with Composure + Presence. Each one you beat can only move on their next turn.

Mana Cost: 6 Speed: Instant Type: Debuff Use: Combat Range: All enemies in sight Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: Composure + Presence Effect: Each enemy resists with Composure + Presence. Each one you beat moves one zone away from you and cannot approach you on their next turn.

Mana Cost: 7 Speed: Instant Type: Debuff Use: Combat Range: All enemies in sight Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: Composure + Presence Effect: Each enemy resists with Composure + Presence. Each one you beat loses their next turn. Each one who beats you still loses 1 AP.

Mana Cost: 7, upkeep 6 each Upkeep Phase Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Enhancement, Persistent Use: Combat Range: Allies in sight who can hear you Dice Pool: Fortitude + Presence + Howling Magic Defense: None Effect: While maintained, each ally adds bonus dice equal to half your Heritage dots, rounded up, to one roll each turn.

From "Peoples of the Known World" by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University The first time I met a Bestial on the Demon Continent, I mistook them for a monster. Most first time visitors make this mistake. Correcting it quickly is better for one's social standing and physical safety. Bestials walk upright, speak, and live in communities with their own traditions. Their animal heritage shows far more than it does in Beastfolk. A Bestial may have the full face of a boar, scaled hide from neck to toe, or a turtle's shell built into the skeleton. They are by far the largest population on the Demon Continent and have been throughout its long recorded history. Political power rests with the Immortal Demon Kings, whose domains have been stable for centuries. Bestials hold little of that power, but in practice they are equal citizens. Some types have well known names. Orcs are porcine: large, direct, and very serious about food. Kobolds are canine: quick, social, and loyal. Tortles are turtle-like: slow, deliberate, and patient enough to make Ogres look impulsive. Reptaurs are lizard-like and cold blooded, so their energy depends on the temperature. Morning meetings with a Reptaur in cold weather go poorly. Lifespan follows the animal. Reptilian types such as Tortles and Reptaurs live about two hundred years. Mammalian types such as Orcs and Kobolds live about one hundred. Mixed settlements are common, so most Bestial communities are used to some neighbors outliving others by generations. Bestials carry the instincts of their animal heritage, as Beastfolk do. A canine Bestial and a canine Beastfolk share certain instinctive patterns despite looking very different. These instincts are part of who they are, not a flaw in character. Bestials know outsiders find them startling. They are not troubled by it. The adjustment is the outsider's to make.

Average Lifespan: 100 years for mammalian types (such as Orcs and Kobolds), 200 years for reptilian types (such as Tortles and Reptaurs). Innate Attribute (choose 1, note Innate on sheet): Strength: For a character whose raw physical power and imposing presence define them. Dexterity: For a character whose predatory speed and agility define them. Innate Flaw - Animalistic Instincts: Same as Beastfolk. Work with your Storyteller to define a specific instinctive weakness tied to your animal type. Attribute Flaw - Social: Social attributes cannot be your Affinity column. They can only be your Standard or Aversion column. Heritage Merit (choose 1, record in Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section): Beast Sense: Gain a free specialty in any ability that reflects a natural heightened sense tied to your animal type. Work with your Storyteller to define which ability and specialty name fits. Feral Surge: Once per combat scene per dot in this merit you may add your dots as bonus dice to a single attack roll, representing a burst of pure animal instinct and ferocity.

Every Bestial carries the animal in their blood, and Feral Blood calls it to the surface. An Orc's tusks, a Kobold's nose, a Tortle's shell, a Reptaur's scales: each type expresses it differently. Work with your Storyteller to describe how each spell looks for your animal type. Primary: Strength + Martial Arts + Feral Blood Secondary: Fortitude + Endurance + Feral Blood Extra mana: Damage only. 1 die per mana, up to your Feral Blood dots or Max Mana Per Turn, whichever comes first.

Mana Cost: 1, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Enhancement, Attuned Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While attuned, your claws, tusks, teeth, or beak count as a weapon with a rating equal to your Heritage dots.

Mana Cost: 1, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Enhancement, Attuned Use: Combat and outside combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While attuned, add your Heritage dots to rolls using your animal type's keenest sense.

Mana Cost: 2, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Defense, Attuned Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While attuned, gain Armor equal to half your Heritage dots, rounded up.

In combat, you know which zone it is in for the rest of the scene.

Mana Cost: 3 Speed: Instant Type: Attack Use: Combat Range: Melee Dice Pool: Strength + Martial Arts + Feral Blood Defense: Target's choice of defense Effect: Move one zone and attack in the same action with no extra AP.

Mana Cost: 3 Speed: Reaction Type: Defense Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: Fortitude + Endurance + Feral Blood Defense: None Effect: When you are attacked, roll your dice pool. Each success removes 1 success from the attacker's roll.

Mana Cost: 4, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Enhancement, Attuned Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While attuned, add your Heritage dots to attack rolls and suffer -2 dice on all other rolls.

Mana Cost: 4 Speed: Instant Type: Attack Use: Combat Range: Melee Dice Pool: Strength + Martial Arts + Feral Blood Defense: Target's choice of defense, then Strength + Athletics to break free Effect: On a hit you also hold the target. A held target cannot move away from you and suffers -2 dice until they beat your successes with Strength + Athletics on their turn.

Mana Cost: 5, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Enhancement, Attuned Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While attuned, add 2 to Strength and Fortitude for all rolls and thresholds.

Mana Cost: 5, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Movement, Attuned Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While attuned, you ignore Difficult Terrain and cannot be Rooted, knocked prone, grappled, or moved against your will.

Mana Cost: 6 Speed: Instant Type: Attack Use: Combat Range: Melee Dice Pool: Strength + Martial Arts + Feral Blood Defense: Target's choice of defense Effect: A hit is treated as meeting the next-higher damage threshold.

Mana Cost: 6 Speed: Reaction Type: Defense Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: Once per scene, when you would become Incapacitated, stay standing and act normally for one more turn.

Mana Cost: 7, upkeep 6 each Upkeep Phase Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Debuff, Persistent Use: Combat Range: All adjacent zones Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While maintained, enemies in range cannot attack anyone but you.

Mana Cost: 7, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Enhancement, Attuned Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While attuned, you take a giant form of your animal. Add your Heritage dots to attack rolls and double your BDT.

Trolls, Bugbears, Minotaurs, Gnolls, Centaurs, and similar. Big, powerful, and frequently underestimated intellectually. From Liris Kant's entry on the monster peoples The Brutes, trolls, bugbears, minotaurs, gnolls, centaurs, and other large peoples of Monsera, are consistently underestimated, especially in intelligence and temperament. I have met a minotaur engineer in Monsera's infrastructure division. They are not an exception. They are what minotaurs are when no one assumes otherwise. Brutes are physically powerful, and for most of them it is the least interesting thing about them.

Average Lifespan: 100 years. Innate Attribute (choose 1, note Innate on sheet): Strength: For a character whose raw physical power and imposing might define them. Fortitude: For a character whose toughness and capacity to absorb punishment define them. Innate Flaw - Imposing: Brutes suffer a penalty die on Expression rolls. Their size and appearance trigger an instinctive wariness in others. Attribute Flaw - Mental: Mental attributes cannot be your Affinity column. They can only be your Standard or Aversion column. Heritage Merit (choose 1, record in Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section): Brute Force: Grants a free specialty in Melee or Martial Arts called Brute Force, reflecting their natural aptitude for leveraging their size and strength in combat. Thick Hide: Grants a free specialty in Endurance called Thick Hide, providing a bonus die against physical damage reflecting their naturally tough and resilient body.

The Brutes are big, and their magic makes them bigger. Titan's Weight is mass made into force: the shove that moves a cart, the stomp that drops a line of soldiers, the body that will not be moved. Primary: Strength + Melee or Martial Arts + Titan's Weight Secondary: Fortitude + Athletics + Titan's Weight Extra mana: Damage only. 1 die per mana, up to your Titan's Weight dots or Max Mana Per Turn, whichever comes first.

Mana Cost: 1, attuned (stays committed) Speed: Instant, Extended Type: Enhancement, Attuned Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: None Defense: None Effect: While attuned, add half your Heritage dots, rounded up, to damage rolls on Strength-based attacks.

Mana Cost: 1 Speed: Reaction Type: Defense Use: Combat Range: Self Dice Pool: Fortitude + Athletics + Titan's Weight Defense: None Effect: When something would move you, knock you prone, or grapple you, resist with this dice pool instead of your normal roll.
