From "Peoples of the Known World" by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University One book changed the world's understanding of the Superd. It was written by a well known Hyuman mage and published to an audience that was not ready for it. Its evidence was too thorough to dismiss. During the Laplace War, the Demon God Laplace persuaded Superd warriors to trade their tail spears for ones he made. Those spears drove them into indiscriminate slaughter. The world blamed the Superd. For centuries few distinguished between a people who chose violence and a people used as a weapon. The Superd paid for that with isolation and fear. I visited their settlement in the old forests of the Biheiril Kingdom, by introduction through local contacts. It is small and carefully kept. The people were among the most deliberate I have met. Every adult carries a trident spear formed from their own forked tail, which hardens and detaches as they mature. Each spear is unique. The spear is the center of Superd identity. They hold that it is the vessel of their soul. This is a spiritual belief, not a physical fact. A Superd who loses their spear can still live and fight, but their community regards them with pity, and among the Superd pity is a heavy judgment. A stolen spear will be recovered at any cost. They are exceptional in combat. Today their reputation is less about danger than luck: many adventurers believe a Superd in the party means things will go well. Every Superd I met was very good at staying alive and keeping others alive, which may explain the belief. In recent decades, younger Superd have begun to travel. Some work in Biheiril's towns. A few have gone further. Their elders view this with pride and some worry. The Superd have a chief and govern themselves through formal authority and long standing consensus. Their political structure is simple. They survived something enormous and remained a people.

Average Lifespan: 1000 years. Innate Attribute (choose 1, note Innate on sheet): Strength: For a character whose warrior might and physical power define them. Composure: For a character whose unshakeable steadiness and calm in the face of conflict define them. Innate Flaw - Spear Sworn: Superd suffer a 1 die penalty on all attack rolls made with anything other than their personal tail spear. This includes unarmed combat, other weapons, and magic used offensively. A Superd who loses their spear will not fight under any circumstances and will willingly accept death rather than raise another weapon. A stolen spear will be recovered at any cost. Attribute Flaw - Social: Social attributes cannot be your Affinity column. They can only be your Standard or Aversion column. Physical Note: All Superd have pale skin, green hair, and a red gem embedded in their forehead functioning as a third eye. They are born with a forked tail that hardens and detaches as they mature, becoming their personal trident spear. Heritage Merit (choose 1, record in Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section): Third Eye: Grants a free specialty in Awareness called Third Eye, providing a bonus die on Awareness rolls to detect living beings and sense the flow of mana in the surrounding area. Soul Spear: Grants a bonus die on all attack rolls made with the character's personal tail spear. The spear itself is indestructible by conventional means and requires Cosmic rank magic to damage.

The red gem on a Superd forehead sees life and mana itself, and the tail spear carries the soul of its owner. Soulbound is the magic of both: sight that nothing living can hide from, and a spear that answers like a limb. Spear Sworn still applies, so Soulbound attacks are made with the personal tail spear. Fairies, Pixies, and similar. Small enough to fit in a coat pocket and fast enough that you might not notice them until they have already gone through it. From Liris Kant's entry on the monster peoples The Tiny peoples, fairies, pixies, and their kin, are the most misrepresented in popular literature, which treats them as whimsical. They vary in temperament like any people. They live in a world not built for their size, and their adaptations, speed, precision, and access to spaces no one else can reach, make them far more capable than most assume. A fairy who fits in a coat pocket can also get into places you would prefer stayed closed.

Charisma: For a character whose outsized personality and magnetic presence define them. Innate Flaw - Tiny: Tiny heritage characters suffer a penalty die on Strength based rolls and cannot wield standard sized weapons without significant penalty. Attribute Flaw - Physical: Physical attributes cannot be your Affinity column. They can only be your Standard or Aversion column. Heritage Merit (choose 1, record in Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section): Hard to Hit: Each dot in this merit adds a bonus die to Dodge rolls. Tiny Terror: Grants a free specialty in Stealth, reflecting their ability to hide in spaces no other heritage could fit.

Glamour is illusion, misdirection, and a little bit of dust that makes the impossible briefly true. From "Peoples of the Known World" by Liris Kant, Third Chair of Natural Philosophy, Monsera University The vampires of the Shaded Isles noble house are currently the most visible of their kind, a result of the isles joining the Monsera kingdom. I have met several members of the royal family, though not the queen. Vampires are sustained by mana, which places them among the Corporeal Undead without making them identical to the others. They do not age while their mana is maintained. They can regenerate mana from emotion as devils do, and they can drink blood, which is their most efficient source. They drink openly and without embarrassment, and the wider world accepts it as a known vampire trait. Sunlight does not destroy them. It drains their mana faster and causes discomfort, so most avoid long exposure. In the Shaded Isles the permanent overcast makes the question moot. Elsewhere they manage it as a known limitation. A vampire colony exists in the far north of the Central Continent, where the sun is absent for much of the year. I have not visited. Travelers describe an insular community, not hostile but not welcoming, that trades occasionally with nearby Hyuman settlements and is otherwise left alone. Every vampire has a compulsion tied to their strongest Virtue or Vice. When triggered, it demands to be satisfied, and resisting it is possible but costly. I have met vampires compelled toward acquisition, toward self sabotage, and toward fixation on a single task. None discuss it casually, and I did not press. Those who spoke of it described living with it rather than having overcome it. Vampires are born or turned. Born vampires grow up with their nature and treat it as a plain fact. Turned vampires come to it through some irreversible event later in life and tend to be more reflective about it, since they remember being something else.

Average Lifespan: Immortal. Sustained by mana. Does not age while mana is maintained. Innate Attribute: Any single attribute of the player's choice. Vampires are as varied in natural ability as Hyumans. That attribute starts at 2 dots and its maximum is raised by 1 beyond the column cap. Note Innate on sheet. Innate Flaw - Compulsion: Every vampire has a compulsion derived from one of their Virtue or Vice extremes. When triggered the vampire must act on their compulsion or take 1 Bashing damage per turn in combat or 1 Bashing damage per scene out of combat until they give in or the trigger is removed. Consult the compulsion table below and work with your Storyteller to determine what specifically triggers yours. Attribute Flaw: None. Like Hyumans, Vampires may place any attribute group in their Affinity column.

Humility: Self Sabotage - compelled to undermine their own success or status in a meaningful way Pride: Dominance Display - compelled to publicly establish superiority over whoever they perceive as challenging them Charity: Ruinous Giving - compelled to give away something of genuine value, money, information, or an advantage they cannot afford to lose Greed: Acquisition - compelled to take something they want whether it belongs to someone else or not Chastity: Denial - compelled to deny themselves something they genuinely want, a pleasure, an indulgence, or a desire they have been holding back Lust: Fixation - compelled to pursue whoever has captured their attention and make moves to claim them as their own regardless of consequences Patience: Paralysis - compelled to wait and do nothing even when action is desperately needed Wrath: Blood Rage - compelled to physically harm whoever triggered their anger Temperance: Abstinence - compelled to refuse all nourishment including blood and mana restoration until the feeling passes Gluttony: Feeding Frenzy - compelled to feed, blood or emotion, from whoever is nearest regardless of consent or consequence Kindness: Bleeding Heart - compelled to help whoever appears to be suffering even if doing so puts themselves or their allies in danger Envy: Sabotage - compelled to undermine or damage something belonging to whoever they envy Diligence: Obsessive Focus - compelled to complete whatever task is in front of them to the exclusion of everything else including immediate threats Sloth: Shutdown - compelled to stop moving, acting, or engaging entirely until the feeling passes A Note on Turned Vampires: A character turned into a vampire through play gains the Compulsion flaw and functional immortality. They do not receive the Innate Attribute benefit or a free dot in a Vampiric Power. Vampiric Powers may be purchased with XP like any other Heritage magic. Heritage Merit (choose 1, record in Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section): Resilience: A dotted merit with no mana cost. Each dot raises the character's BDT by 1 beyond the normal calculation.

Vampiric Powers are the Heritage magic of vampires. Unlike other heritages, vampires have five of them: Auspex, Blood Sorcery, Celerity, Dominion, and Vigor. A born vampire chooses one Vampiric Power and receives its free dot. The others can be bought with XP like any Heritage magic, at dot x5, each with its own Awakening. Turned vampires receive no free dot. Resilience, once counted among the Vampiric Powers, is now the vampire Heritage Merit and costs no mana.

Older generations call them Blessings and Curses; modern science calls them Merits and Flaws. Both are understood to be the same ambient magic that touches every newborn, simply with different outcomes. A Merit is something the world handed you that helps. A Flaw is something the world handed you that does not. Neither was asked for, and neither can be bought or removed with XP after character creation. At character creation you have 7 points to spend on Merits. You may take up to 7 points of Flaws, and each Flaw point adds 1 point to your Merit budget, for a possible total of 14. Any points left unspent carry over to your Backgrounds in Step 8. Your Heritage Merit from Chapter 8 is recorded here too, but it is free and does not use any of these points. Because Merits and Flaws never change with XP, it helps to fill your Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section from the bottom up for Merits and Flaws, and from the top down for Backgrounds. That keeps the two visually apart and easy to read at a glance.

Before spending any Merit points, consider whether your character needs to go beyond the normal maximums, or would happily accept a weakness in exchange for strength elsewhere. You may raise or lower the maximum of any single Attribute, or of any Ability group, by spending or recouping Merit points. The cost or refund is always the larger of the two numbers involved. Raising: Raising a maximum by 1 costs points equal to the new maximum. Raising Intelligence from a maximum of 5 to 6 costs 6 points. Raising it again to 7 costs 7 more, for 13 in total. This is expensive on purpose. Lowering: Lowering a maximum by 1 refunds points equal to the current maximum. Lowering Manipulation from a maximum of 4 to 3 refunds 4 points. Ability groups: The same rules apply. Lowering a Noble group valued at 2 down to a maximum of 1 refunds 2 points. Raising a Mage group valued at 5 to a maximum of 6 costs 6. Adjustments only change what a trait can reach later through XP. They do not change how many dots you spend at creation, and the Golden Rule still stops anything from being filled above 5 during creation. Note raised maximums as Max Boost 1, Max Boost 2, and so on next to the Attribute, and lowered maximums as Max Loss 1, Max Loss 2. For an Ability group, change the number written next to the group. Write a short note explaining each adjustment so you and your Storyteller can track them.

A player wants a sword mage, equally dangerous with blade and spell. They make Physical their Affinity column (6) and Mental their Standard column (5), so Intelligence can only reach 5. They want it to reach 7. Raising to 6 costs 6 and raising to 7 costs 7 more: 13 points, more than their budget of 7. Social is their Aversion column (4), and Manipulation does not matter to this character, so they lower its maximum from 4 to 3 and recoup 4 points. They also lower the Noble group from 2 to 1 and recoup 2 more. That gives them 6 extra points, which with their starting 7 makes exactly 13. They note Max Boost 2 next to Intelligence and Max Loss 1 next to Manipulation, and change the Noble group's number from 2 to 1. They still spend 5 points in the Mental column and 2 dots in the Noble group at creation, and Intelligence still cannot be filled above 5 until play begins. After that, it can grow all the way to 7.
Costs are listed per dot unless a set cost is given. A merit's maximum is the most dots you can take in it.

Merit Cost Effect Ambidextrous 2 No penalty for using your off hand in combat or for fine work. Bonus Aggravated Health 4 for 1 box, 7 for 2 Unlocks one or both of the dotted Aggravated health boxes on your sheet. Bonus Lethal Health 3 for 1 box, 5 for 2 Unlocks one or both of the dotted Lethal health boxes on your sheet. Gifted Athlete 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to Athletics rolls and rolls to push your body physically. Iron Will 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds 1 dot of Willpower. Keen Senses 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to Perception rolls. Natural Armor 4 per dot, max 3 Scales, hide, or tough skin. Each dot adds 1 to your BDT like armor, without wearing any. It stacks with worn armor. Quick Reflexes 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to Initiative rolls (Dexterity + Perception). Resilience 2 per dot, max 7 Each dot adds 1 to your damage threshold (your BDT, and so your LDT and ADT as well). Survivor's Grit 2 per dot, max 5 Each dot adds a bonus die to rolls to resist environmental hazards, starvation, extreme conditions, and anything that pushes you to the edge of what you can endure.

Merit Cost Effect Animal Kinship 2 per dot, max 3 Animals trust you. Each dot adds a bonus die to rolls to calm, handle, or ride animals and beasts. Born Negotiator 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to Commerce and Diplomacy rolls made to strike a deal. Come Back 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to spoken rolls in social combat. You may also use a sharp remark to start social combat outside a fight. Commanding Voice 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to rolls to give orders, rally allies, or take charge in a crisis. Disquieting Presence 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to Presence rolls. Your eerie nature draws attention whether you want it or not, and it is not always welcome. Honest Face 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to rolls to be believed when you are telling the truth. Natural Leader 2 per dot, max 3 Once per scene, give one ally bonus dice equal to your dots on a single roll you helped plan. Silver Tongue 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to Persuasion rolls. Social Butterfly 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to social rolls in group settings. Striking Looks 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to social rolls where your appearance matters.

Merit Cost Effect Calm Mind 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to rolls to resist Sanity damage. Danger Sense 2 Once per scene the Storyteller may warn you of danger before it strikes, even without a roll. Direction Sense 3 You always know which way you are facing and can retrace any path you have traveled. Eidetic Memory 2 Perfect recall of anything you have directly experienced. It does not grant knowledge you never had. Encyclopedic Knowledge 3 Once per scene, in any field where you have at least 1 dot in the matching ability, ask the Storyteller one factual question your character could plausibly know and get a true answer. Iron Focus 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to rolls to resist distraction, fear, and magic that affects the mind. Jack of All Trades 4 You never roll fewer than 1 die for an ability you have no dots in. Multilingual 2 per dot, max 5 Each dot grants fluency in one more language. The languages of Terrana are Hyuman Tongue, Demon Tongue, Beast Tongue (with dialects including Elven and Dwarven), Sky Tongue, Sea Tongue, and Dragon Tongue. Sharp Mind 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to Intelligence rolls to solve puzzles, codes, and problems. Tactical Mind 3 Once per combat, during the Planning Phase, give one ally 1 AP that does not come from your own.

Merit Cost Effect Arcane Ward 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to rolls to resist spells. Aura Sensitivity 2 per dot, max 3 Sense the emotional state and rough power of beings nearby. Each dot increases the range and accuracy. Deep Well 4 Regain 1 extra mana during each Upkeep Phase. Elemental Kinship 2 per dot, max 3 Choose one casting school. Each dot adds 1 to your BDT against that school's attacks. Leyline Sense 2 You always know the direction of the nearest strong source of mana, such as a dungeon, a ley line, or a Void Opening. Magical Affinity 5 One free dot in Mana or in a single Magical Knowledge of your choice. A knowledge taken this way gets a P. Mana Reservoir 2 per dot, max 5 Each dot adds 2 to your Mana Pool. Spell Memory 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot lets you prepare one more spell beyond your Intelligence. Spell Touched 2 per dot, max 3 Trace magic from a past event lingers in your body. Each dot adds a bonus die to rolls with one Magical Knowledge chosen at creation. Steady Focus 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to rolls to keep a persistent spell going when you are hurt or distracted.

Merit Cost Effect Familiar Bond 2 per dot, max 3 A creature is magically bonded to you. Each dot increases its capability and the depth of the bond. Choose the creature with Storyteller approval. Fast Healer 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot lets you heal 1 extra Bashing damage whenever you take a short or long rest. Fey Touched 3 per Gift, max 2 Gifts One parent was Fey or a devil. Choose Gifts from the Fey Touched list below. Hard to Kill 4 Once per story arc, when you would mark your last Aggravated box, you do not mark it. Lucky 5 Once per story arc, reroll any single roll entirely. Magic Eye 5, or 7 for a greater eye One of Kishirika's Magic Eyes. Choose from the list below. Only one at creation. Night Eyes 2 You see in darkness as well as in dim light. Old Soul 2 You remember more than one life. Choose a second Past Life Occupation. Second Wind 3 Once per combat, neutralize 2 Bashing damage without spending an action. Youthful Charisma 2 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a bonus die to social rolls where seeming innocent, harmless, or younger than you are helps.

Empress Kishirika Kishirisu is famous for gifting her Magic Eyes to those who earn her favor. A character can begin play with one through the Magic Eye merit, or receive one from Kishirika during the story. A Magic Eye replaces one of your eyes and can be opened or closed at will. While open it is attuned: it holds 1 mana committed against your Maximum Mana Per Turn. Closing it returns that mana in your next Upkeep Phase. Foresight, Absorption, All-Seeing, and Absolute Void are greater eyes and cost 7 points. The rest cost 5.

Eye Cost Effect Mana Perception 5 See mana itself: spells, enchantments, mana flows, and roughly how much mana a being holds. Identification 5 Look at an item or creature to learn what it is. The Storyteller gives you one key fact each time you look. X-Ray 5 See through solid matter, up to your Perception in zones. Clairvoyant 5 See a place you know as if you stood there, anywhere in the same region. You are blind to your own surroundings while you look. Foresight 7 Glimpse a moment ahead. Add 2 bonus dice to every defense roll while the eye is open. Absorption 7 When a spell hits you, roll Composure + Attunement. Each success reduces the spell's damage by 1 and adds 1 mana to your pool. All-Seeing 7 See in total darkness, through illusions and invisibility, and in every direction at once. You cannot be surprised. Absolute Void 7 Spend 4 mana to turn one zone you can see into an unbreakable barrier until your next turn. Nothing passes through it, including attacks and spells. Tracking 5 Follow the trail of anyone you have seen, through any terrain, if the trail is no more than a day old. Superd 5 See living things by their life force, even through walls, and know whether each one means you harm. Affection 5 Anyone who meets your gaze is drawn to like you. Add 2 bonus dice to social rolls with them; they resist with Composure.

A character with one Fey or devil parent and one parent of any other heritage is Fey Touched ( Chapter 8 ). They live about 400 years whatever their other parent's lifespan, and they may carry a little of the otherworld in them. Each Gift costs 3 points, up to 2 Gifts. Wings: You have wings and fly at double your normal movement. Record a free specialty in Athletics called Flight. Second Bloodline: You may raise your other parent's Heritage magic with XP, starting at 0 dots, following all the normal Heritage magic rules. Fey Sight: You can see fey, spirits, and glamours that are hidden from ordinary eyes. Fey Charm: Add a bonus die to Expression and Performance rolls meant to enchant or enthrall an audience. Otherworldly Look: A feature of your choice marks your heritage: horns, a tail, unusual eyes, or something stranger. Add a bonus die to Presence rolls to unsettle or impress.
Each Flaw point adds 1 point to your Merit budget, up to 7 Flaw points in total.

Flaw Points Effect Addiction 1 per dot, max 5 You need a substance or experience to function at your best. Each dot makes the dependency, and going without, worse. Blind 7 You cannot see. Sight-based rolls are impossible or made at a severe penalty. Other senses may compensate over time with Storyteller approval. Chronic Pain 1 per dot, max 3 Once you take any damage in a scene, each dot adds a penalty die to your physical rolls for the rest of it. Clumsy 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a penalty die to Dexterity rolls that need quick or delicate movement. Deaf 5 You cannot hear. Hearing-based rolls are impossible, and social rolls that depend on speech suffer heavy penalties. Frail 1 per dot, max 2 Each dot removes one of your Lethal health boxes. Glass Jaw 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot lowers your BDT by 1. Missing Limb 3 for a hand or foot, 5 for an arm or leg Effects depend on the limb and the Storyteller. Automaton prosthetics are common in Terrana, and some people prefer them. Sickly 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a penalty die to rolls to resist disease and poison. Slow 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot lowers your Initiative by 1.

Flaw Points Effect Awkward 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a penalty die to social rolls with strangers. Dark Secret 1 per dot, max 4 Something you are hiding. Each dot raises how bad it is and what happens if it comes out. Debt 1 per dot, max 3 You owe someone powerful. Each dot raises the size of the debt and the threat of not paying. Enemy 2, 3, or 5 (1 to 3 dots) A named enemy who grows more powerful with each dot. The Storyteller controls them and brings them in at dramatic moments. Honest to a Fault 3 You cannot tell a deliberate lie. Subterfuge rolls to deceive automatically fail. Infamous Family 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a penalty die to social rolls with anyone who knows your family name. Notoriety 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a penalty die to social rolls with groups who know your bad reputation. Outcast 1 per dot, max 3 Your own people have cast you out. Each dot adds a penalty die to social rolls with your heritage or home community. Sworn Rival 2 Someone your equal is determined to beat you and keeps turning up to try. The Storyteller controls them. Ward 1 per dot, max 3 Someone depends on you completely. Each dot makes them more vulnerable and more trouble.

Flaw Points Effect Absent-Minded 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a penalty die to rolls to remember details, plans, or where you left things. Amnesia 2 to 5 (1 to 4 dots) Gaps in your memory. Each dot makes them larger and more of your past unreachable. Compulsion 1 per dot, max 4 A behavior you cannot easily resist. Each dot makes it trigger more often and harder to suppress. Gullible 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a penalty die to Insight rolls to spot a lie. Haunted 2 to 4 (1 to 3 dots) Something follows you: a spirit, a curse, a recurring event. It worsens with each dot, and the Storyteller controls it. Insomnia 1 per dot, max 2 Each dot lowers the Bashing damage you heal from a long rest by 1. Nightmares 1 per dot, max 2 Each dot lowers the Willpower you regain from rest by 1. Paranoid 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a penalty die to rolls to trust or work with others, including helping them. Phobia 1 per dot, max 4 An irrational fear of something specific. Each dot makes it more crippling when triggered. Reckless 2 You must pass a Composure roll to retreat or hold back from danger.

Flaw Points Effect Cursed 2 to 7, set with the Storyteller A magical curse of the Storyteller's design. At 2 points it is an inconvenience; at 7 it defines your life. Magic Averse 1 per dot, max 7 Each dot locks you out of one of the seven casting schools. Choose them at creation with Storyteller approval. Mana Beacon 2 Your mana can be sensed from far away. Spirits, voidlings, and anyone hunting magic find you more easily. Mana Deficient 1 per dot, max 5 Each dot lowers your Mana Pool by 2. Mana Leak 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot drains 1 mana from your pool during every Upkeep Phase. Mana Sensitive 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot adds a penalty die to all rolls in areas of high ambient mana, and mana sickness affects you sooner. Slow Channel 1 per dot, max 3 Each dot lowers your Maximum Mana Per Turn by 1. Unstable Magic 1 per dot, max 3 Your spells can misfire. At 1 dot, a casting roll with three or more 1s misfires; at 2 dots, two or more; at 3 dots, any 1. The Storyteller decides what goes wrong. Void Touched 3 You were exposed to Void energy. Voidlings notice you more readily, and you take a penalty die on rolls to resist Void effects. Wild Mana 2 Whenever you add extra mana to a roll, roll one die. On a 1 the extra mana is spent but adds nothing.

Some characters arrive with something that fits no standard category: a power so specific and so significant that it defines them. These are the big ones, the potentially game-changing ones, borrowed from other stories, other worlds, or invented from scratch. Special Powers cost 7 points per dot, with a maximum of 2 dots at creation (14 points). Whether more dots can be bought with XP later is entirely up to the Storyteller. Storyteller approval is required for everything in this section, and the Storyteller may change costs, add conditions, or say no if a power does not fit the campaign. A power this big rarely comes without strings. Consider pairing it with the Devil's Bargain flaw.

Power Cost Effect Devil's Fruit 7 per dot, max 2 Inspired by One Piece. A single transformative power of the Logia, Paramecia, or Zoan type. The player proposes it and the Storyteller sets it. You cannot swim without a heavy penalty. Shadow Monarch 7 per dot, max 2 Inspired by Solo Leveling. Raise defeated enemies as shadow soldiers whose strength scales with your dots. Requires at least 1 dot in Shade Magic. Bankai Potential 7 per dot, max 2 Inspired by Bleach. Your main weapon holds a dormant spirit. Awakening it in play unlocks a powered-up form designed with the Storyteller. Titan Shift 7 per dot, max 2 Inspired by Attack on Titan. Transform into a massive, powerful form for a number of turns per session equal to your dots. You are exhausted when it ends. Cursed Energy 7 per dot, max 2 Inspired by Jujutsu Kaisen. A personal cursed technique designed with the Storyteller. At higher ranks each use costs 1 Sanity. Nen Awakening 7 per dot, max 2 Inspired by Hunter x Hunter. Your Nen is awakened as an Enhancer, Emitter, Transmuter, Conjurer, Manipulator, or Specialist, and your type shapes a unique ability designed with the Storyteller. Witch Factor 7 per dot, max 2 Inspired by Re:Zero. You carry the essence of one of the Witches of Sin: extraordinary power tied to that sin, with consequences that grow the more you use it. Breath Style 7 per dot, max 2 Inspired by Demon Slayer. A breathing technique that floods your body with power for a number of turns per scene equal to your dots, with extra effects against monsters and demons. Designed with the Storyteller. Unique Skill 7 per dot, max 2 Inspired by That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime. A gift from your arrival in Terrana, such as an analysis voice like the Slime King's Great Sage, or a skill that devours and copies what it consumes. Designed with the Storyteller. Devil's Bargain (Flaw) 3 to 7 points back, 1 to 3 dots Pairs with the powers above. You gained something extraordinary and owe something in return: a debt, a limit, or a weakness built into the power. Define it with the Storyteller.

Arcane Enhancements, or augmentation, are a special merit open to every character, but they are most common in the Corporate Kingdoms of Shirone, Kikka, and Sanika on the Central Continent, where back-alley augmentation shops make them easier to get than anywhere else in the world. Each enhancement is its own merit with its own cost, recorded as a separate entry in your Merits section. You may take up to two enhancements at creation. More can be added later at the Storyteller's discretion. In the Corporate Kingdoms, part of the XP cost is replaced by in-game costs, such as jobs, debts, or trades with whoever performs the work, so the XP cost there is lower than anywhere else. The body's magical channels have limits, and augmentation permanently takes up part of that capacity. Every enhancement lowers your Maximum Mana Per Turn by 1. Heavy enhancements lower it by 2. A bonus dot from an enhancement is added on top of the trait. It does not change the trait's own dots, so the Golden Rule does not limit it, and it can take a trait past its normal cap. Note Arcane next to the trait on your sheet and write the bonus in its bonus space.

Enhancement Cost Effect Prosthetic Limb 4 A working automaton limb that replaces a lost one and removes the Missing Limb penalty. Filter Lungs 4 Immune to airborne poisons and gases, and you can hold your breath for 10 minutes. Optic Implants 4 See in darkness, and add a bonus die to sight-based Perception rolls. Skill Chip 4 +1 bonus dot to one Ability. Reinforced Bones 5 +1 to your BDT. Hidden Blade 5 A retractable weapon built into your arm. It cannot be disarmed and passes searches. Spring Legs 5 Leap one zone straight up or over an obstacle as part of your move. Muscle Weave 6 +1 bonus dot to Strength or Fortitude. Reflex Wiring 6 +1 bonus dot to Dexterity or Perception. Neural Link 6 +1 bonus dot to Intelligence or Wisdom, and you can interface directly with implements. Subdermal Plating 7, heavy +2 to your BDT. It stacks with worn armor. Jump Jets 8, heavy Mechanical flight at double your movement. You must use all of your movement every turn or begin to fall. Mana Capacitor 8, heavy Stores up to 5 mana outside your pool, which you can draw on in any turn.

Backgrounds are the circumstances of your character's life rather than anything inside them. Attributes describe your body and mind, and Abilities describe what you have learned. Backgrounds describe what surrounds you: the people who know you, the resources you can draw on, the reputation you carry, and the networks you move through. They are not you, but they shape what you can do in the world in ways raw ability cannot. Spending Points: At character creation you have 7 points to spend on Backgrounds, plus any points left over from Merits and Flaws. Freebie Points can also buy Backgrounds at 1 point per dot. Backgrounds are rated up to 7 dots, but no Background can be filled above 5 at creation. Resources: Every character starts with 1 free dot of Resources, the basic financial footing any working person in Terrana has. More dots are bought normally. After Creation: Backgrounds cannot be bought with XP. The Storyteller may award Background dots for what you achieve in play: relationships built, resources won, reputations earned. On Your Sheet: Fill Backgrounds from the top of the Merits, Flaws, and Backgrounds section downward, so they stay apart from your Merits and Flaws, which fill from the bottom up. Guild Standing is recorded under Guilds and Memberships on your OurSpace page. The list below covers the most common circumstances. If your concept needs a resource or relationship not on it, work one out with your Storyteller. Some Backgrounds, such as Hacker and Subscribers, belong to the modern era and may not exist in games set in another era.

Like nearly everything in the game, Backgrounds are rated from 1 to 7 dots, and 7 dots is truly enormous. No Background can be filled above 5 at character creation, and 5 is already very high by most measures. Dots 6 and 7 are only reached through play.

Background Description Allies Reliable people who will actively help you when asked. Define each ally's field or affiliation at creation. Each dot is either a new ally or a more powerful one. 1 dot is a capable friend; 3 dots is someone with real power or several solid friends; 5 dots is a person of major influence who will go to bat for you. 7 dots is one of the most powerful people in the world in your corner. Allies have their own lives and limits. They are not servants. Contacts People who feed you information in a chosen field. They will tell you things, but they will not take risks for you. Each dot is a broader network or a deeper source. 1 dot is a single useful source; 3 dots covers a city's worth of whispers in your field; 5 dots means little in your field happens without you hearing of it. 7 dots is an intelligence network that rivals a kingdom's. Fame How widely you are known, and for what. 1 dot is local recognition in one community; 3 dots is a name known across a continent in your field; 5 dots is a name that opens conversations in places you have never been. 7 dots is a name known in every corner of Terrana, a living legend. Fixer Someone who works outside normal channels and makes things happen: finding work, solving problems quietly, and connecting people. 1 dot is a local fixer for small jobs; 3 dots can find serious work and make big problems vanish within a region; 5 dots has reach across continents. 7 dots can arrange almost anything, anywhere, for the right price. A fixer has their own interests and their own prices. Followers People personally loyal to you or your cause, not hired staff. They take risks that Contacts will not, but they are not trained soldiers or specialists. 1 dot is a handful of devoted friends; 3 dots is a small movement; 5 dots is a following large enough to fill a town square. 7 dots is a movement that spans nations. Hacker Your skill at getting into and moving through the CCN and the crystal-based systems that run the modern world. Hacking has existed in any real form for only twenty to thirty years. 1 dot is basic access and navigation; 3 dots gets you through most secured systems with time and patience; 5 dots reaches systems their builders believe are unreachable. 7 dots treats the CCN itself as an open book. Every use needs tools and time, and the Storyteller decides what is possible. Influence Pull within one institution, organization, or power structure, defined at creation. 1 dot opens doors that would otherwise stay closed; 3 dots gets real favors done; 5 dots means the institution moves when you push it. 7 dots means you effectively control it. Mentor A more experienced person invested in your growth. Each dot reflects both their power and how committed they are to you. 1 dot is a capable teacher with limited reach; 3 dots is a respected master; 5 dots is someone the whole world pays attention to. 7 dots is one of the Seven Strongest, or someone of that standing. Nobility You were born into a noble family. 1 dot is minor local nobility with a small estate and a name that matters in one town; 3 dots is an established house with regional reach; 5 dots is high nobility with continental recognition and political weight. 7 dots is a literal monarch or head of state, such as a king or president. Resources Wealth, income, and lifestyle. Every character starts with 1 free dot. 1 dot is a modest life: a one-bedroom apartment or a dorm room and the basics covered; 3 dots is wealthy by most standards; 5 dots is generational wealth or a major business. 7 dots is wealth on the scale of a Corporate Kingdom. Monthly income, starting funds, and the cost of living are in Chapter 14 ; track the money you have on hand next to Resources on your sheet. Retainers Staff, employees, or trained assistants in your service. Unlike Followers they are professionals: they do the job well, but their loyalty is to the job. Each dot is more retainers or more capable ones. 1 dot is a single assistant; 3 dots is a small skilled staff; 5 dots is a household or company of experts. 7 dots is an organization of hundreds working for you. Safe House Secure places to hide, rest, or lie low. Dots can make one location better or, if you say so at creation, add more locations. 1 dot is a single clean, hidden spot with basic supplies; 3 dots is well equipped for a long stay with some defenses; 5 dots is a fortified, fully supplied base for long-term concealment. 7 dots is a hidden stronghold no one has ever found. Street Cred Respect within a community or scene you define with the Storyteller. It does not have to be criminal: deep roots in a neighborhood or real standing in an underground scene both count. 1 dot is local respect; 3 dots carries weight across a city or region; 5 dots means people who have never met you know what you stand for. 7 dots makes you a legend of your scene worldwide. Subscribers An engaged audience that follows you on the CCN, as a creator, public figure, or someone whose life simply caught people's attention. 1 dot is a modest local following; 3 dots is an audience across several regions; 5 dots is reach large enough to move public opinion. 7 dots is one of the biggest names on the CCN. Fame is general recognition; Subscribers is an audience that follows your output. You can have either without the other.

Guilds are how the modern world organizes itself, and in Monsera they are the government: every citizen 18 or older may join one, and membership is how a citizen gains a political voice. Seats in the parliamentary cabinet are divided among the ten cabinet guilds. Guilds also operate outposts well beyond Monsera. Guild Standing measures your rank and pull within one guild. Take it separately for each guild you belong to, and record each one with its dots under Guilds and Memberships on your OurSpace page. Being a member at all is free and needs no dots; Guild Standing is what makes the guild work for you. Limits: Guild Standing is rated from 1 to 7. The Storyteller sets how many dots can be bought in each guild at creation; in most games the limit is 3 dots in any one guild. Higher standing is earned in play. The Hero Rangers Corps: The HRC is not a cabinet guild, but it works like one for this Background. Your Guild Standing in the HRC is your rank in the Corps, from Rank 1 trainee to Rank 7 Titan candidate ( Chapter 3 ).

Dots Standing 1 Member in good standing. You can use the guild's halls, job boards, and services, and other members treat you as one of their own. 2 Respected. You are known within your local chapter, trusted with better work, and can call on fellow members for small favors. 3 Officer. You hold a recognized post in your chapter, can vouch for others, and have a say in local guild business. 4 Chapter head. You lead a local chapter or outpost and can direct its members and resources. 5 Regional leadership. You help run the guild across a region or continent. 6 High council. You sit on the guild's highest council and shape its direction worldwide. 7 Guild head. You lead the guild and hold its seat in Monsera's cabinet.

Guild Members and Work Adventurers Delvers, monster hunters, and explorers. Runs job boards, outposts, and bounties throughout the world. Arts Performers, artists, writers, and entertainers, from street musicians to CCN stars. Farmers Growers, ranchers, and food producers who feed Monsera and its trade partners. Hero Rangers Corps Monsera's military corps against the Rift and its Kaiju, with outposts in every nation. Standing is your Corps rank. Healers Doctors, clinics, and healing mages, including curse removal and advanced care. Laborers Builders, haulers, miners, and the workers who keep the city running. Mages Spellcasters, enchanters, and magical researchers. Keepers of the heptagram. Makers Smiths, engineers, and crafters of implements, machines, and gear. Merchants Traders, shopkeepers, bankers, and the moneyed interests of Monsera. Navigators Sailors, pilots, guides, and anyone who moves people and goods across land, sea, and sky. Scholars Researchers, archivists, teachers, and translators. Thieves (unofficial) Extralegal and unrepresented, with no cabinet seat. Speaks its own secure dialect, Thieves' Cant. Its members do not advertise their standing.

Willpower, Fate, Sanity, and Mana sit outside the normal attribute and ability system. Willpower, Fate, and Sanity are never bought with Freebie Points or XP; they are built and lost through play. Mana is the exception: it can be bought, but only at a steep price. Together these four stats describe the deeper texture of who your character is and what the world asks of them across a campaign. Every character starts with 5 dots each in Willpower, Fate, and Sanity (Willpower may start at 4 or 6, depending on your highs), and 1 dot of Mana.

Willpower, Fate, and Sanity are each tracked with a row of 10 dots and, beneath it, a row of 10 boxes. The dots are your rating: it can never go above 10. The boxes are a running record of what has happened to that stat in play. They do not reset when you rest, after a session, or at the end of a story chapter. They only change when new marks are added. A box can be in one of three states: blank, checked, or marked with an X. Checks: Gains, growth, and healing are marked with checks, filling the row from left to right. X's: Damage, spending, and loss are marked with X's, filling the row from right to left. A Mixed Row: When the row is full of checks and X's together, a new check replaces the X nearest the checks, and a new X replaces the check nearest the X's. Each side pushes against the other. A Full Row: When all 10 boxes are checks, gain 1 dot. When all 10 are X's, lose 1 dot. Either way, erase every mark in the row and start fresh. Dots can only change through a full row (and a few Merits, Flaws, and Storyteller awards). None of the three can ever go above 10 or below 1. Like an attribute, the last dot can never be lost: a full row of X's at 1 dot is erased, but the dot stays.

Willpower is your character's mental and emotional resilience. It is the resource you spend when you need to push past your limits, and the health track you protect when someone tries to break you with words instead of weapons.

Willpower starts at 5 dots. If both of your highs are Vices, it starts at 4; if both are Virtues, it starts at 6; one of each leaves it at 5. The Iron Will Merit adds 1 dot per dot of the Merit, up to 3. After creation, moving on the scales never changes your Willpower dots.

You can spend 1 Willpower per turn. Spending it takes no action. Mark 1 X and choose one: Push: Before a roll, add 3 dice to it. Reroll: After a roll, reroll up to 3 failed dice. You can keep spending even when your row is mostly X's. If the row fills with X's, you lose a Willpower dot and erase the row. Some Battle Aura techniques at Rank 4 and higher can be paid with Willpower instead of mana ( Chapter 13 ). That payment is separate from this once-per-turn spend, and each point still marks an X.

Willpower damage marks X's, the same as spending. It comes from: Social combat: Willpower is the health track for social combat (see below). Acting against your scales: Any violation at a Low Virtue or Low Vice, and minor violations at a High position, cost Willpower ( Chapter 7 , Part 2). Small scale shifts: When the Storyteller moves one of your scales a short way.

In social combat, the attacker rolls a Social Attribute plus a relevant Ability. The defender rolls Willpower plus Composure. Each success the attacker has over the defender deals 1 Willpower damage. How each side acts can earn bonus or penalty dice from their scales. A social combat ends when either side fills their row with X's (losing a Willpower dot, or erasing the row at 1 dot), or when 5 or more damage is dealt in a single retort. A defender who rolls 5 or more successes over the attacker makes a Critical Comeback: the attacker loses momentum and the exchange ends in the defender's favor.

Resting does not erase X's. Willpower is regained by earning checks, which push the X's back. The Storyteller awards checks when your character acts meaningfully on their Driving Factors or Trope, holds firm on what they believe at a real cost, or takes genuine time off to do things they love after a demanding job. A session where a character fully embodies their drive earns more than one where they only touched on it. Fill the whole row with checks and you gain a Willpower dot.

Fate is your character's karmic weight in the world: how deeply they are woven into the story of Terrana and how much they can bend it. Where Willpower is for tackling the thing right in front of you, Fate is your ability to weave the world's story in your favor, and to stand against outcomes that seem preordained. Fate is not spent. It is built and lost through how much influence your character has in the world.

Player characters start at 5 dots simply by being reincarnates: arriving in this world from another is itself a significant karmic event. The average person has about 3. Kings and other figures of great worldly power typically have 8 or more. Death itself has a Fate of 10.

Checks: Making plans that succeed, striking and keeping deals, taking opportunities, forming ties with important people, and engaging with the forces that shape history. X's: Plans that fail, broken deals, opportunities ignored, refusing the requests of powerful people, and losing a Fate contest. A full row of checks gains a Fate dot; a full row of X's loses one. Fate can never fall below 1.

When your character works with the flow of the world, asking it for something it has no reason to refuse, the Storyteller should generally let Fate carry the moment without a roll. A dying friend getting to see the flowers bloom one more time is a story the world is willing to tell. When your character pushes against something with its own Fate, the two meet in a Fate contest.

Both sides roll their Fate dots as a dice pool. The side with more successes gets its way; the defender wins ties. The winner marks a check and the loser marks an X. Opposing Fate can be pooled. A character trying to stop a death rolls against Death's 10. A character trying to stop an arranged royal wedding rolls against the combined Fate of the two kingdoms behind it, which may be 16 dice or more. Challenging the groom to a duel instead is not a Fate contest at all; it is just a duel. Fate is fickle. Pushing against forces far heavier than you is a quick way to lose it, and learning when Fate is worth testing is part of the game.

Sanity is your character's connection to reality, their psychological stability, and their capacity to process what the world puts in front of them. Most of Terrana can be managed. Voidlings are different: their existence is hostile to the ordered mind, and parties that face them regularly need to look after each other. Sanity damage accumulates differently from physical or social damage and heals differently. Lost Sanity changes who the character is, not just what they can do. Your Sanity dots are also your dice pool for resisting Voidling horror and other Void effects.

Sanity damage marks X's. It comes from: Severe violations at a High position: acting fundamentally against a High Virtue or High Vice ( Chapter 7 , Part 2). Significant scale shifts: when the Storyteller moves a scale a long way. The Void: exposure to Voidlings and Void phenomena, whatever happens to the body. Resisting a compulsion: sustained resistance to a vampire's compulsion without resolution. Some powers: a few Merits and spells cost Sanity to use.

Sanity heals by living life and having fun, marked with checks. What heals the mind varies from person to person, so this is intentionally broad: acting on your Driving Factors over time, spending real time with people you care about, or some form of therapy that fits the character. That might be an actual therapist, a fortune teller, a night drinking with friends, a hot spring, or a creative hobby. The Storyteller decides how many checks it earns based on how genuinely the character engaged, not just whether they went through the motions.

Every character starts at 5 Sanity. When a full row of X's costs a dot, the player and Storyteller give the character a mental trauma shaped by what caused the loss. It may change how they interact with the world, and it grows more extreme the lower Sanity falls. 5 or higher: Stable. No trauma. 4: A phobia or lasting quirk tied to what caused the loss. 3: A serious trauma that shapes how the character acts and reacts. 2: A severe trauma that can take over in moments of stress. 1: The player loses control. The Storyteller runs the character until long-term care brings them back. Sanity can never drop below 1. Like an attribute, losing the last dot would mean the character no longer exists.

A full row of checks gains a dot and a deeper, more resilient hold on reality. Recovering a dot can soften or remove a trauma. At 10, the character's grasp of reality is so complete that they no longer see the world the way ordinary people do. The player loses control, and the Storyteller runs the character.

Everything in Terrana carries mana: rocks, trees, insects, rivers, and the air between things. It is the fundamental substance of the world and the medium magic moves through. Anyone raised here has at least 1 dot from growing up surrounded by it. To someone who arrives with none, the same ambient mana is closer to poison.

Mana is rated from 1 to 10 dots, the only trait with ten. Every character starts with 1. At creation it can only be raised with Freebie Points, at 7 points per dot, and the Golden Rule still applies. After creation, each dot costs the new dot x7 in XP. Mana counts toward your Level.

Mana Pool = (Magic dots + Circle Magic dots) x Mana. With no dots in Magic or Circle Magic, your pool is 0. Some items let other abilities, such as Alchemy, Attunement, or Implements, count too. The Mana Reservoir Merit and Mana Deficient Flaw adjust the pool.

Max Mana Per Turn (M/T) = Fortitude + Mana. This is the most mana you can safely spend in one turn, however large your pool is. Upkeep costs paid during the Upkeep Phase count toward it. Attuned effects and items hold part of it for as long as they are active, and some Arcane Enhancements lower it permanently.

Mana pays for spells, techniques, and other magical effects. Mana can also enhance a roll at 1 die per mana, declared before rolling and assigned to the attack or the damage roll. Spending mana to boost anything is always limited to your dots in that magic or combat ability, or your M/T, whichever comes first.

Attuned: Artifacts, augmentations, and attuned default abilities hold part of your M/T while active. No further mana is needed to use them. Committed: Persistent effects cost their upkeep (the spell's cost minus 1) every Upkeep Phase, and that upkeep counts toward your M/T. Ending an attuned or committed effect returns that mana to your M/T during the following Upkeep Phase.

A character who spends their pool down to 0 drops unconscious and is Incapacitated until they recover mana. A character whose pool is 0 only because they have no dots in Magic or Circle Magic is not affected.

In combat you recover mana during each Upkeep Phase, based on your Mana dots, plus 1 if you took damage since your last turn. Recovery never takes you above your pool. Outside combat, a few minutes of rest refills the pool, so unless a party fights battle after battle without a break, they start every encounter full. Mana Dots Per Upkeep Phase 1 to 3 1 mana 4 to 6 2 mana 7 to 8 3 mana 9 4 mana 10 5 mana Took damage +1 mana

You may choose to spend more than your M/T in a single turn, but every mana over the limit burns. Filling all of your Aggravated boxes through Mana Burn knocks you incapacitated immediately. Any Mana Burn that deals even 1 Aggravated leaves a permanent Mana Burn mark; what it looks like, how visible it is, and whether it changes anything are up to the Storyteller. Repeated burns can leave lasting deformities. Over M/T Damage 1 1 Bashing 2 1 Lethal 3 1 Aggravated 4 2 Aggravated 5 or more 3 Aggravated, +1 per mana over 5

1 dot of Mana covers the world's baseline density comfortably. Some places are far denser: ancient magical sites, areas near Void openings, and places where something significant happened to the local mana. Elevated density deals Bashing damage; extreme concentration deals Lethal. The Storyteller decides what counts as elevated or extreme. Direct summons from other worlds who arrive with no Mana take Bashing damage from the world itself until they develop 1 dot through play.

Voidlings feed on mana. Ambient mana sustains them at a basic level, but strong Mana signatures draw them. A party with several high-Mana characters in Void-adjacent territory should expect concentrated Voidling attention.
When a character dies without choosing to, the mana they held counts down by 1 each day, and resurrection is possible until it runs out ( Chapter 13 ).

Not every fighter in Terrana casts spells. Sword schools, fight pits, hunting lodges, and drill yards all pass down their own ways of fighting, and a master of one is as dangerous as any mage. A Combat Style is one of those traditions: a single form of combat, trained from the first lesson to mastery. Each Style covers one form, such as short blades, polearms, or boxing. Every dot teaches something new, in a fight or outside one. The knife fighter learns to skin game before learning to throw a blade, and the wrestler learns to work a crowd long before the piledriver. Styles are built to pair with Battle Aura, which pours fighting spirit into whatever Style a character practices.

Ranks: A Style has seven dots, named on the Rank Scale used across the character sheet: Elementary, Intermediate, Advanced, Saint, Royal, Imperial, and Divine (F through S). Pools: Every Style lists a Primary pool, used for its attacks, and a Secondary pool, used to defend or support. Both are an Attribute plus an Ability. What Each Dot Gives: Every rank has a Default Ability and two Options. When you buy the dot, you gain the Default Ability and pick Option A or Option B for free. The option you did not pick is not lost: you can buy it later for Rank x2 XP, without raising the Style again. Use: Every entry is marked Combat, Outside combat, or Both, the same as spells. Your Dots: When an entry says "your dots," it means your dots in that Style. A bonus to your own rolls or an ally's rolls equals your dots. A bonus to BDT equals half your dots, rounded up. Penalties a technique puts on an enemy never scale: they stay at the flat amount written.

At Creation: In Step 10, your Physical column decides how many Combat Style dots you spend: 7 for Affinity, 5 for Standard, or 3 for Aversion. Spread them across any Styles you like. The Golden Rule applies, so no Style can go above 5 dots at creation. Mark every Style you take in this step with a P for Primary. Freebie Points: Combat Style dots cost 4 Freebie Points each. A new Style bought with freebies is marked with an S for Secondary. XP: A Primary Style costs the new dot x5. Any other Style costs the new dot x6. The option you did not pick at a rank costs Rank x2 XP. Divine and the God Titles: Reaching the Divine rank makes you one of the finest practitioners alive, but titles such as Sword God or Water God are not ranks of a Style. They are won and held ( Chapter 5 ).

Style Form Primary Pool Secondary Pool Quickcut Style Short Blades Dexterity + Melee Dexterity + Stealth Silver Arc Style Long Blades Dexterity + Melee Perception + Dodge Timberfall Style Axes Strength + Melee Fortitude + Endurance Heron's Reach Style Polearms Dexterity + Melee Perception + Awareness Wallguard Style Shields Strength + Melee Fortitude + Endurance Ten Count Style Boxing Strength + Martial Arts Fortitude + Endurance Drifting Leaf Style Kung Fu Dexterity + Martial Arts Perception + Dodge Main Event Style Wrestling Strength + Martial Arts (or Athletics) Fortitude + Endurance Windreader Style Bows Dexterity + Ranged Perception + Awareness Sundown Style Hand Guns Dexterity + Ranged Perception + Awareness Iron Rain Style Large Guns Fortitude + Ranged Strength + Athletics

Zones: Only one creature or object can be in a zone. Melee attacks reach adjacent zones, so "all adjacent zones" means everyone right next to you. A charge or leap always ends in an empty zone. One Attack Roll: A technique that hits several targets, or the same target several times, still makes a single attack roll. Each target, and each strike, defends against that roll separately. Counter: When your defense roll beats an attack, a Counter lets you strike back using that same defense roll as your attack roll. The attacker defends normally, and has to be within reach of your weapon. Armor Penetration: BDT is Fortitude + Armor, plus Resilience if you have that Merit, plus any magic that raises it. Armor Penetration lowers the Armor part of the target's BDT by the amount listed, for your hit only, and their LDT and ADT drop with it. Full Armor Penetration ignores the whole Armor part. It never lowers Fortitude or Resilience. Magic Penetration: Works the same way on the magic part of a BDT: points added by spells, enchantments, or magical gear. Stacking Penetration: Penetration from different sources adds together, but neither kind can take its part of a BDT below 0. Lowering Armor: Some techniques lower a target's Armor for the rest of the scene. That damages their gear, so it helps everyone attacking them, unlike Armor Penetration, which only applies to your own hit. Called Shots: Aiming at a specific limb, weapon, or vital spot costs -2 dice on the attack roll. Its effect only happens if the attack hits. Range: Melee weapons hit adjacent zones, or one zone farther with Reach. Thrown weapons go up to double your Strength in zones. Bows, guns, and ranged spells can hit anywhere you have line of sight to; half cover gives -2 dice ( Chapter 14 ). Conditions: Bleeding, Prone, Rooted, and Grappled work as written in the Conditions rules. A Bleeding effect from a Style has a rating equal to your dots. When a technique makes a target lose AP on their next turn, that is how a stun works in Terrana.

Battle Aura is built to work with every Style. Its attack techniques roll the Attribute + Ability of the Style you are fighting with, plus your dots in that Style. With its second dot, Battle Aura gives Aura Edge, an attuned ability that adds Armor Penetration and Magic Penetration to your weapon and unarmed attacks. Aura Edge stacks with any Armor Penetration your Style gives ( Chapter 13 ).

Small blades: get close, cut what matters, and be gone before the other side reacts. Covers: daggers, knives (skinning knives and work knives too), stilettos, short swords, throwing knives. Primary Dexterity + Melee Secondary Dexterity + Stealth Default Ability Skinner's Hands Outside combat You're skilled at field-dressing, skinning, butchering, and knife work (whittling, cutting rope, scraping hides). Add your dots to rolls to skin or harvest a creature. Each success also saves one extra usable part (hide, sinew, horn, or gland). Option A Quick Hands Combat Drawing or swapping to a short blade costs no AP. Add your dots to initiative if you start combat with one in hand. Option B Find the Gap Combat Add your dots to attack rolls against a target that hasn't acted yet this round. Default Ability Throwing Edge Both You can throw any short blade using this Style's Primary pool, at a target up to double your Strength in zones away. It works outside a fight too, to hunt small game or cut a rope. Option A Twin Grip Combat Wield a short blade in each hand. When you attack with both, add your dots to that one attack roll. Option B Pin and Run Combat When a thrown blade hits, spend 1 AP to pin the target's clothing or foot. They're Rooted until the end of their next turn. Default Ability Hidden Steel Both You get one extra Belt slot (slot 4), which can only hold short blades. Drawing from it costs no AP. Add your dots to rolls to keep a blade hidden when you're searched. Option A Opening Cut Combat On a hit, spend 1 AP to give the target Bleeding, at a rating equal to your dots. Option B Slip Away Combat After you make a melee attack, move 1 zone for free. Default Ability Butcher's Eye Outside combat One look tells you how a creature is put together and where it's weak. Add your dots to rolls to cut out poison, treat a wound with a knife, or track something you've wounded. Option A Weak Point Combat Once per round, a short blade hit has Armor Penetration equal to half your dots. Option B Dancer's Step Combat Add your dots to defense rolls against an adjacent enemy you've hit this round. Default Ability Fan of Knives Combat One thrown attack can target up to three creatures within throwing range, using one attack roll. Option A Second Strike Combat If your attack roll beats the target's defense by 3 or more successes, add your dots to the damage. Option B Ghost Step Combat Once per round, when your defense roll beats an adjacent attack, make a Counter with a short blade, then move 1 zone for free. Default Ability Unseen Approach Both Add your dots to Stealth rolls. Your first hit on a target that hasn't noticed you counts as meeting the next-higher damage threshold. Option A Severing Strike Combat A called shot that hits a limb gives the target -2 dice on rolls using that limb for the rest of the scene. Option B Breath Cut Combat Spend 2 AP: on a hit, the target also loses 2 AP on their next turn. Default Ability Every Edge Is Mine Both Anything with an edge or point (a glass shard, a broken sword, a sharpened spoon) counts as a short blade for you, with a Rating equal to your dots. Option A Death of a Thousand Cuts Combat Spend 3 AP: one attack roll against every enemy in all adjacent zones. Each one you hit also gets Bleeding, at a rating equal to your dots. Option B The Last Mercy Combat Once per story, a hit on a target at their -4 wound penalty or worse automatically meets their ADT.

The sword schools: reading an opening and closing it before the other side reacts. For a two-handed greatsword, you may use Strength + Melee as the Primary pool. Covers: longswords, sabers, katanas, rapiers, broadswords, greatswords. Primary Dexterity + Melee Secondary Perception + Dodge Default Ability Sword Sense Outside combat One look tells you a blade's quality, balance, and maker, and you can sharpen, maintain, and care for any sword. Add your dots to rolls to appraise or repair a blade. Option A Clean Line Combat Add your dots to an attack roll made right after moving 1 zone. Option B High Guard Combat Add your dots to defense rolls on any round you don't attack. Default Ability The Salute Outside combat You know the dueling customs of Terrana's sword schools. A formal challenge from you has to be openly answered or openly refused. Add your dots to social rolls about duels, honor, and exhibition bouts. Option A Riposte Combat Once per round, when your defense roll beats an adjacent melee attack, make a Counter. Option B Bind Combat On a hit, spend 1 AP to tie up the target's weapon. Their next attack roll takes a flat penalty die. Default Ability Versatile Grip Combat Switch between a one-handed and two-handed grip for free. Two-handed, add half your dots to damage. One-handed, your other hand is free for a shield or an item. Option A Twin Blades Combat Wield a long blade in each hand. When you attack with both, add your dots to that one attack roll. Option B Disarming Edge Combat On a hit, spend 1 AP to make the target drop their weapon into an adjacent zone. Default Ability Named Strike Both Name your signature cut. Once per scene, add your dots to its damage. Anyone who has seen it before recognizes your school, which helps your reputation and ruins disguises. Option A Crossing Cut Combat One attack roll against two adjacent enemies. Option B Perfect Parry Combat Once per scene, a failed defense roll against a melee attack counts as a success. Default Ability Duelist's Name Outside combat Anyone who knows sword work knows you. Add your dots to social rolls to impress or intimidate them. Option A Blade Dance Combat Spend 2 AP: one attack roll against every enemy in all adjacent zones. Option B Unbroken Rhythm Combat Once you've hit the same target three times in a row this scene, add your dots to all your attack and defense rolls against them for the rest of the scene. Default Ability Cut the Unseen Both Your blade can strike and harm incorporeal and conjured things as if they were solid, and can cut what usually can't be cut (smoke-forms, webs of spun magic). Option A Unseen Line Combat Once per scene, the target can't add bonus dice from any source to their defense against this attack. Option B Return Stroke Combat When your defense roll beats a melee attack by 3 or more successes, make a Counter. This is in addition to any other Counter you have. Default Ability Master of the School Outside combat You're recognized as a sword master. You may found a school, and anyone who trained under you can call on your name. Option A One Thousand Schools Combat Spend 3 AP: move up to 2 zones and make one attack roll against every enemy you pass adjacent to. End in any empty zone along your path. Option B One Perfect Cut Combat Once per story, a hit that meets BDT counts as meeting ADT.

Heavy, committed swings that break shields, dent armor, and end a fight in a hit or two. Covers: hatchets, hand axes, battle axes, bearded axes, greataxes. Primary Strength + Melee Secondary Fortitude + Endurance Default Ability Woodsman's Grip Outside combat You can fell trees, split logs, clear brush, and build simple shelters and fires in half the usual time with an axe. Add your dots to rolls to cut through wood, doors, or barricades. Option A Heavy Hands Combat Add your dots to damage while wielding an axe in two hands. Option B Hook and Pull Combat On a hit, spend 1 AP to hook the target with your axe head. Either pull them 1 zone toward you into an empty zone, or yank their shield aside so they lose its Armor bonus until their next turn. Default Ability Toss the Hatchet Both You can throw hatchets and hand axes using this Style's Primary pool, up to 2 zones. Option A Shield Breaker Combat A hit on a shield-bearer lowers that shield's Armor bonus by 1 for the rest of the scene. This stacks. Option B Second Wind Combat After you take damage, spend 1 AP to add your dots to your next attack roll this round. Default Ability Battle Rhythm Outside combat Woodchopping contests, lumberjack feats, work songs, war chants. Add your dots to rolls for feats of strength, or to keep a work crew or war band moving. Option A Cleave Combat One attack roll against your target and one other adjacent enemy. Option B Momentum Combat If you only moved last round and didn't attack, add your dots to this round's attack roll. Default Ability Splitter Both Your axe has full Armor Penetration against doors, barricades, wooden walls, and other objects. One hit breaks open an ordinary wooden door. Option A Armor Breaker Combat On a hit, the target's Armor drops by 1 for the rest of the scene. This stacks. Option B Rooted Stance Combat Add your dots to rolls to resist being pushed, knocked Prone, or Rooted. Default Ability Woodsman's Legacy Outside combat With an axe and timber, you can build a raft, a palisade, or a footbridge in a few hours instead of days. Option A Wide Arc Combat Spend 2 AP: one attack roll against every enemy in all adjacent zones. Option B Bone Breaker Combat A called shot that hits a limb gives the target -2 dice on rolls using that limb until it's healed. Default Ability Unstoppable Swing Combat Once per scene, an attack has full Armor Penetration. Option A Felling Blow Combat A hit that meets LDT also knocks the target Prone. Option B Berserker's Due Combat While you're at your -2 wound penalty or worse, add your dots to damage. Default Ability Timber Both One swing fells anything that grew or was built from wood: a gate, an old tree, a ship's mast. Outside combat this takes no time at all. In combat it costs 3 AP. Option A The Woodsman's Judgment Combat Spend 3 AP: one attack roll against every enemy in all adjacent zones. Everyone you hit is knocked Prone. Option B World Splitter Combat Once per story, a hit has full Armor Penetration and counts as meeting the next-higher damage threshold. The target's weapon or shield also breaks.

Reach and spacing: control the distance and the fight is already decided. Covers: spears, pikes, halberds, glaives, naginata, tridents, quarterstaffs. Primary Dexterity + Melee Secondary Perception + Awareness Default Ability Reach Combat With a polearm, you can attack targets up to 2 zones away, not only adjacent ones. Option A Herder's Staff Outside combat Add your dots to rolls to herd animals, fish with a spear, or test ice, mud, or deep water ahead of you. Option B Held Line Combat Add your dots to attack rolls against an enemy who moved into your reach this round. Default Ability Pole Vault Both Once per round, vault on your polearm to move 1 extra zone. You can clear a gap, a low wall, or a Prone body this way. Option A Sweep Combat A low strike knocks the target Prone instead of dealing damage. Option B Push Back Combat A hit also pushes the target 1 zone away from you. Default Ability Standard Bearer Outside combat A banner on your polearm draws people to you. Add your dots to rolls to lead, signal, or hold a group together. Option A Set Against the Charge Combat When an enemy who moved this round attacks you, add your dots to your defense roll. If your defense beats their attack, make a Counter. Option B Cutting Line Combat One attack roll against two enemies in a straight line within your reach. Default Ability Phalanx Combat You and any adjacent ally holding a polearm or shield each add half your dots to defense rolls. Option A Pin Combat On a hit, spend 1 AP to leave the target Rooted until the end of their next turn. Option B Whirling Guard Combat On a round you don't attack, make one defense roll, adding your dots, and use it against every melee attack made on you that round. Default Ability Long Reach Combat Your Reach extends to 3 zones. Option A Lever and Lift Outside combat Use your polearm as a lever or pole. Add your dots to rolls to pry open gates, lift a portcullis, or knock down something high. Option B Zone Denial Combat An enemy within your reach has to spend 1 extra AP for each zone it moves away from you. Default Ability Unyielding Combat An enemy you've hit this round can't push you, Root you, or knock you Prone. Option A Line Breaker Combat Spend 2 AP: one attack roll against every enemy in a straight line out to the end of your reach. Option B Piercing Thrust Combat A hit on a Rooted or Prone target has full Armor Penetration. Default Ability Heron's Patience Both You can stand perfectly still for hours. You notice anything that moves within your reach, even while resting, and it can't catch you by surprise. Add your dots to Awareness rolls. Option A The Unbroken Spear Combat Spend 3 AP: one attack roll against every enemy within your reach. Option B Sky Piercer Combat Once per story, throw your polearm like a javelin at any target you can see. It hits automatically and counts as meeting the next-higher damage threshold.

A shield used as both wall and weapon, protecting the people next to you as much as yourself. Covers: bucklers, round shields, kite shields, tower shields. Primary Strength + Melee Secondary Fortitude + Endurance Default Ability Watchful Guard Outside combat Bodyguard work, sentry duty, watching a camp. Add your dots to Awareness rolls to spot threats to someone you're protecting. Option A Sturdy Stance Combat While holding a shield on a round you don't attack, add half your dots to your BDT. Option B Shield Bash Combat Attack with your shield using this Style's Primary pool. A hit pushes the target 1 zone away. Default Ability Cover Ally Combat Spend 1 AP: an adjacent ally adds your dots to their next defense roll this round. Option A Hold the Line Combat Add your dots to rolls to resist being pushed, knocked Prone, or moved. Option B Arrow Catcher Combat Add your dots to defense rolls against ranged attacks. Default Ability Shield Wall Combat While an adjacent ally also holds a shield, you both add half your dots to your BDT. Option A Turtle Combat On a round you take no Action, make one defense roll, adding your dots, and use it against every attack made on you that round. Option B Dent the Plate Combat A hit with your shield lowers the target's Armor by 1 for the rest of the scene. This stacks. Default Ability Steady the Line Both Add your dots to rolls to lead a defense. Adjacent allies add your dots to rolls to resist fear. Option A Counter Bash Combat Once per round, when your defense roll beats a melee attack, make a Counter with your shield. Option B Interpose Combat Once per round, when an adjacent ally is hit, you take the hit instead, and your BDT applies. Default Ability Shield Throw Combat Throw your shield using this Style's Primary pool, up to 3 zones. A hit pushes the target 1 zone. The shield rebounds to your hand at the start of your next turn. Option A Unbreakable Guard Combat Once per scene, a hit that would meet your LDT counts as meeting only your BDT. Option B Bulwark Combat Cover Ally now protects every adjacent ally for the same 1 AP. Default Ability Ride the Shield Both Ride your shield down a slope, snowbank, or staircase, or float on it as a small raft. In combat, one adjacent ally behind it adds your dots to defense rolls against ranged attacks. Option A Ram Combat Move up to 2 zones in a straight line and make one attack roll against the first enemy you reach. On a hit they're pushed 1 zone and knocked Prone. Option B Ricochet Throw Combat Your Shield Throw can hit two targets with one attack roll, bouncing from one to the other. Default Ability Living Wall Combat An enemy has to spend 1 extra AP to move into any zone adjacent to you. Option A The Last Wall Combat For the rest of the scene, you can redirect any attack against an adjacent ally onto yourself, adding your dots to your defense roll against it. Option B Unbroken Combat Once per story, while you hold your shield, you can't be Incapacitated this scene. Damage that would Incapacitate you leaves your last Health box empty instead.

The fist style built for damage: footwork, combinations, and taking a punch to land a better one. Covers: bare fists, wraps, gloves, knuckle-dusters, cestus. Primary Strength + Martial Arts Secondary Fortitude + Endurance Default Ability Iron Chin Both Add your dots to rolls to resist being knocked out, losing AP, or being intimidated by physical threats. Option A Jab Combat On a hit, spend 1 AP for a second strike on the same target, which they defend against using that same attack roll. Option B Bob and Weave Combat Add your dots to defense rolls against fists and melee weapons. Default Ability Roadwork Outside combat Running, skipping rope, hours of training. Add your dots to Athletics rolls for long runs and hard exertion. You don't tire from a long march or a chase. Option A Body Shot Combat A hit also makes the target lose 1 AP on their next turn. Option B Guard Up Combat While fighting unarmed, add half your dots to your BDT against unarmed attacks. Default Ability Prize Fighter Outside combat Add your dots to rolls to win over a crowd, talk up a fight, or read the odds on one. Option A Combination Combat If your attack roll beats the target's defense by 3 or more successes, a follow-up punch adds your dots to the damage. Option B Cut Off the Ring Combat On a hit, the target has to spend 1 extra AP to move away from you on their next turn. Default Ability Cornerman Outside combat You know how to patch up cuts and swelling. Outside combat, each success on your roll heals as Basic healing, Bashing damage only. Option A Haymaker Combat Spend 1 AP to add your dots to damage. If you miss, take a flat penalty die on defense rolls until your next turn. Option B Counterpuncher Combat Once per round, when your defense roll beats an adjacent attack, make a Counter. Default Ability Granite Jaw Combat Your Bashing wound penalties count one step lower (-1 becomes none, -2 becomes -1, -4 becomes -2). Option A Liver Shot Combat On a hit, the target takes a flat penalty die on every roll until the end of their next turn. Option B Barrage Combat Spend 2 AP: one attack roll strikes the same target three times, and they defend against it three times. Default Ability Ring Sense Combat Add your dots to initiative. No one within 2 zones of you can catch you by surprise. Option A Knockout Blow Combat A called shot to the head that hits makes the target lose 3 AP on their next turn. Option B Rope-a-Dope Combat Each attack that misses you this round adds 1 die to your next attack roll, up to your dots. Default Ability Champion's Belt Both Add your dots to social rolls anywhere fighting is respected. Once per story, you can declare a fight a sanctioned bout, and most people will honor its rules. Option A Final Bell Combat Spend 3 AP: one attack roll strikes the same target a number of times equal to your dots, and they defend against each strike separately. Option B Down for the Count Combat Once per story, a hit that meets LDT on a target at their -2 wound penalty or worse knocks them out (Incapacitated).

The fist style built for avoiding hits: flow, redirected force, and never being where the blow lands. Covers: open-hand forms, palms, kicks, sweeps.
